Article labels repeat, so `article` needs a `corpusType` from one of those two families, `STATE_CONSTITUTION` also needs `state`, and `STATE` / `REGULATION` need the `code`. A request missing one is refused with 422 before anything is charged. String or list.
article.title: Article

changedSince.description:
Only return sections we have OBSERVED change on or after this date (`YYYY-MM-DD`). This is the sync filter: it turns a lookup API into something a nightly job can poll, without creating a board watch per jurisdiction.

These are observed changes, not effective dates. A refresh compared the publisher against the copy we held and found it different; the date is when we SAW it, an upper bound on when it took effect. It is the same event stream `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}/changes` serves per section, so a hit here has a history there.

Coverage is bounded by capture, not by the age of the law. Change capture began long after the corpus did, it is per-source, and events are swept at 5 years. An empty result means no captured change in the window, never that nothing was amended.

Narrow with `corpusType` and `state` for a tighter window: the change set is resolved to concrete sections before the search runs, and a window matching too many sections is rejected with a 422 that says so rather than silently truncating your answer.
changedSince.title: Changedsince

chapter.description: Scope a search to one or more chapters within a title or code, e.g. `21` for USC Title 42 Chapter 21. This is the search-side of the `parent` object on each result: pass a hit's `parent.chapter` straight back to search that hit's neighbors. Chapter numbers repeat across titles, so pair it with `titleNumber` (USC) or `code` (state); an unpaired chapter is rejected. String or list.
chapter.title: Chapter

code.description:
Restrict to specific state statutory codes, e.g. `tx_pe` for the Texas Penal Code. Values are the `identifier`s returned by `GET /us/statutes/divisions?corpusType=STATE&state=XX`, so the browse output can be fed straight back in. Pass a list to search several codes, across states if you like (`["tx_pe", "ca_pen"]`). This is the only way to scope below a whole jurisdiction: `state=tx` alone searches every Texas code at once.

With `corpusType=FEDERAL_RULES`, a value can instead be a federal rule set as `GET /us/statutes/divisions?corpusType=FEDERAL_RULES` lists it: `frcp`, `fre`, `frcpsuppadm`, or an appendix copy such as `uscapp_t28a_fre`. Without that corpusType a bare `frcp` is refused, because it cannot be told apart from a state code missing its state.
code.title: Code

corpusType.description: Restrict to one corpus, or to several by passing a list (`"corpusType": ["USC", "CFR"]`). One of: `USC` (United States Code), `CFR` (Code of Federal Regulations), `STATE` (state statutory codes; call `/us/statutes/coverage` for the list of ingested jurisdictions), `CONSTITUTION` (U.S. Constitution), `FEDERAL_RULES` (FRCP / FRCrP / FRE / FRAP / FRBP), `STATE_CONSTITUTION` (state constitutions; call `/us/statutes/coverage` for the current jurisdiction list), `STATE_RULES` (state court rules; see `/us/statutes/coverage`), `EXECUTIVE_ACTION` (Federal Register Presidential Documents), `REGULATION` (state administrative regulations; pair with `state`), `FEDERAL_REGISTER` (Federal Register agency rules, final and proposed), `AGENCY_GUIDANCE` (sub-regulatory federal agency guidance, 53 named sources spanning the tax, banking, securities, labor, immigration, health-privacy, export-control, intellectual-property, antitrust, energy and communications agencies; each is independently filterable with `source`, which lists them all), `STATE_AGENCY_GUIDANCE` (state-issued regulatory guidance, currently state Department of Insurance bulletins and circular letters; pair with `state`, and see `/us/statutes/coverage`), `SENTENCING_GUIDELINES` (US Sentencing Guidelines Manual), `US_TAX_TREATY` (US income tax treaties and protocols), `US_TREATY` (treaty and international agreement text from the Statutes at Large, U.S.T. and Bevans, plus the Senate ratification record), `SESSION_LAW` (US Statutes at Large: federal public and private laws AS ENACTED, 1789 to date. This is the source the US Code is compiled from, so a section's `publicLawCites` resolve here to the enacting text; call `/us/statutes/coverage` for the live section count), `FEDERAL_LOCAL_RULES` (Federal local court rules), `FEDERAL_REGISTER_NOTICE` (Federal Register notices that act on a rulemaking), `STATE_AG_OPINION` (Formal written opinions of a state Attorney General, construing that state's own statutes, constitution and...), `STATE_REGISTER` (State administrative register NOTICES), `STATUTE_COMPILATION` (Statute compilations), `AGENCY_ADJUDICATION` (Federal administrative adjudications and executive-branch legal opinions, one filterable `source` per body), `CFR_ANNUAL` (GPO's PUBLISHED ANNUAL EDITIONS of the Code of Federal Regulations, 1996 to date), `USC_ANNUAL` (GPO's PUBLISHED ANNUAL EDITION of the United States Code, retired here when the live Code cut over to OLRC...), `FEDERAL_BILL` (Congressional BILLS and resolutions of the 119th Congress, as printed by GPO), `FEDERAL_RULES_ANNUAL` (PAST TEXTS of the national Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Criminal Procedure, Evidence, Appellate...), `FEDERAL_RULES_PROPOSED` (PENDING AMENDMENTS to the national Federal Rules, one document per rule per Rules Enabling Act cycle...). Omit to search across all corpora. The `enum` on this field is the complete token list, and `/us/statutes/coverage` serves a one-line description of each in its legend.
corpusType.title: Corpustype

documentType.description: Federal Register document stage: `final` (a rule in force), `proposed` (an NPRM), or `presidential` (a Presidential Document, the `EXECUTIVE_ACTION` corpus). The same distinction appears in each row's `actId` prefix (`FR_RULE_` vs `FR_PRORULE_`).
documentType.title: Documenttype

excerptChars.description: Characters of matching text to include in each result's `excerpt`, 100 to 600. The excerpt is a ranking preview, deliberately too short to stand in for the section; use `/us/statutes/section/{actId}/body` (or `includeBody`) for the full text. Default 500. A larger value is a 422.
excerptChars.title: Excerptchars

excludeRepealed.description:
Drop sections whose own status says they are no longer operative: repealed, renumbered, transferred, recodified, rescinded, revoked, expired, superseded, omitted, reserved, and the rest of the dead and not-operative vocabulary (the full set is the one behind each result's `goodLawStatus`).

This removes what we KNOW is dead. It does not promise the remainder is good law. A section survives this filter when its status is `in_force` OR when we hold no trustworthy repeal signal for its jurisdiction, and those two are not the same thing. Read `goodLawStatus` on each surviving result to tell them apart: `good_law` is checked, `unknown` is unchecked. Filtering on the status we store and reporting the verdict we derive are deliberately separate, because only the first is indexable.

The United States Code is served from a stored annual edition (`year` 2024, `currentThrough` 2025-01-06), so a section repealed after that edition closed still carries `actStatus: in_force` and survives this filter. Every USC result therefore reports `goodLawStatus: unknown`, which is the honest answer and the one this field's second paragraph tells you to read. Use `/section/{actId}/changes` for the timeline on a section you depend on.
excludeRepealed.title: Excluderepealed

fields.description: Return only these result fields, e.g. `["title", "excerpt"]`. A result carries 40+ fields and most are null on any given row, so a full page of 50 ships a lot of nulls. `actId` and `citation` are always included, because a row without them cannot be used or attributed. Unknown names are rejected with 422 so a typo does not silently drop a field you needed. Omit for the full object. The `required` list on the result schema describes the full object; a response narrowed with `fields` carries only the fields you named.
fields.title: Fields

includeBody.description:
Return the full text of every hit inline, on each result's `body`, instead of making you fetch it per section afterwards.

Why it exists. Search returns a ranking preview, so the alternative is a search call plus one `/section/{actId}/body` call per hit. This collapses a whole page to a single round trip.

Cost: the 4-credit search PLUS the ordinary 6-credit body price for each row that actually returns text. Ten rows with text is 4 + 60 = 64 credits. A row whose text cannot be resolved comes back with `body: null` and is not charged, so read `creditsConsumed` rather than computing it from `limit` -- it is the same price as fetching them yourself, so this buys latency, not a discount.

⚠️ It multiplies with `limit`. `limit: 50` with this set is 304 credits in a single call. Page deliberately.

`includeBody` wins over `fields`: if `fields` omits `body`, `body` is added to it (and `notes` says so), so every body you are billed for is in the response.

Prefer this over raising `excerptChars`: the excerpt is windowed around the match and can begin mid-section, dropping a leading subsection marker, so it is not safe to quote. `body` is the publisher's text.
includeBody.title: Includebody

includePinpoint.description:
Name the subsection each hit matched, in a `pinpoints` object keyed by `actId`. Search ranks whole sections, and a section can run to dozens of subsections; with this set, a hit for `30 mph urban district speed limit` comes back with `625 ILCS 5/11-601(c)(1)`, its own text, the lead-in it completes and its character offsets in the section's `plain` text.

Cost: none. The price is the search price and `creditsConsumed` does not change. It never changes which sections are returned, their order or their scores, and it never fails the search: a hit whose subsection cannot be named says why in `reason` and is still a real match. A subsection is named only when your query's words point at it, so a question put in other words than the law's gets `located: false` rather than a guess.

Time: adds the time to read each returned section's text, usually a few hundred milliseconds for a page of 10. Pinpoints for a large page stop after a few seconds, and the hits not reached say `not_looked_up`.
includePinpoint.title: Includepinpoint

limit.description: Number of results to return per page.
limit.title: Limit

matchType.description:
Controls exact vs. semantic matching. `any` (default) is hybrid semantic + keyword ranking and suits natural-language questions. Use `all` for strict keyword matching (every query word must appear in the text) or `phrase` for an exact-phrase match (the query's words, contiguous and in order). Both match whole words, case-insensitively, ignoring punctuation: `act` does not match `fact`, `10b-5` matches `10b 5`, and `§ 1983` matches `section 1983`. Both are answered from the full text of every section in scope, so a section holding the words is found however the relevance ranking would have placed it, and they page like `boolean`.

`boolean` reads `query` as a terms-and-connectors expression and returns only sections that satisfy it, judged over each section's full text, ranked by relevance among them. Operators are UPPERCASE: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` (`negligence NOT criminal`), `/p` same paragraph, `/s` same sentence, `/N` within N words (1-255), `+p` `+s` `+N` the same with the first term first, `atleastN(term)` at least N occurrences, `"exact phrase"`, and bare words side by side are also an exact phrase (`summary judgment`). Wildcards: `retaliat*` or `retaliat!` (any letters or digits), `wom?n` (one character), with at least 3 characters first. Group with `( )`. Precedence follows the convention of legal research services: `OR` binds tightest, then `/N`, `/s`, `/p`, then `AND`, then `NOT`. A malformed expression is a 422 naming the problem and its position, and is not charged; the response's `parsedQuery` shows how the expression was read. To pull up one specific section, pass its citation as the query with `any` (e.g. `42 U.S.C. § 1983`) and it resolves to that section at rank 1.
matchType.title: Matchtype

offset.description: How many results to skip, for paging. Every page of a given query is cut from one ranking, so results never repeat or go missing between pages, and a later page costs no more than the first. `any` ranks one bounded pool of about 60 sections plus up to about 30 more from the law-specific legs, so roughly 60 to 90 results are reachable and `hasMore` turns false at the end of that pool, which can be before `offset` 70. `offset` is at most 70 there. For exhaustive paging use `matchType: "boolean"`, `all` or `phrase`, which page to the end of the matches (up to 10,000): follow `nextOffset`.
offset.title: Offset

part.description: Scope a search to one or more parts within a title, e.g. `240` for 17 C.F.R. Part 240. The CFR counterpart to `chapter`: pass a hit's `parent.part` straight back to search within that part. Pair it with `titleNumber`; an unpaired part is rejected. String or list.
part.title: Part

publishedFrom.description: Only return Federal Register documents published on or after this date (`YYYY-MM-DD`). This is the PUBLICATION date, which is not the same as `yearFrom`: that filters the version year of a section.
publishedFrom.title: Publishedfrom

publishedTo.description: Only return Federal Register documents published on or before this date.
publishedTo.title: Publishedto

source.description:
Scope to one or more of the following. The named source within `corpusType`, for corpora that fold several independently filterable bodies of law into one token.

`FEDERAL_RULES` sources: `frcp` (Federal Rules of Civil Procedure), `frcrp` (Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure), `fre` (Federal Rules of Evidence), `frap` (Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure), `frbp` (Federal Rules of Bankruptcy Procedure), `sct` (Rules of the Supreme Court of the United States).

`CFR` sources: `far` (Federal Acquisition Regulation (48 C.F.R. ch. 1)), `dfars` (Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 C.F.R. ch. 2)) (both are already part of `CFR`; this only splits the existing Title 48 data by chapter, it does not add new sections).

`AGENCY_GUIDANCE` sources: `administrative_guidance` (Synthesized administrative guidance (e.g. SALT cap, CTC, 401(k) limits)), `ssa_ruling` (Social Security Administration Rulings), `irs_rev_proc` (IRS Revenue Procedures), `irs_notice` (IRS Notices), `irs_rev_rul` (IRS Revenue Rulings), `irs_announcement` (IRS Announcements), `irs_irm` (Internal Revenue Manual (IRS internal procedure)), `merger_guidelines` (DOJ & FTC Merger Guidelines (2023)), `doj_leniency` (DOJ Antitrust Division Leniency Policy), `doj_business_review` (DOJ Antitrust Division Business Review Letters (1991-2021)), `cms_iom` (CMS Medicare Internet-Only Manuals (instruction to Medicare contractors, not a regulation)), `copyright_circular` (US Copyright Office Circulars), `copyright_compendium` (Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices, Third Edition (2014, 2017 and 2021 editions)), `doj_justice_manual` (DOJ Justice Manual), `uscis_policy_manual` (USCIS Policy Manual), `mpep` (USPTO Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP)), `tmep` (USPTO Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP)), `cftc_staff_letter` (CFTC Staff Letters (no-action, exemptive, interpretative; 2008-present)), `fincen_ruling` (FinCEN Administrative Rulings), `fincen_guidance` (FinCEN Guidance (alerts, advisories, notices, bulletins, fact sheets)), `fincen_boi_faq` (FinCEN Beneficial Ownership Information FAQs), `fincen_boi_rule_qa` (FinCEN BOI Rulemaking Q&As (final rule and interim final rule)), `fincen_boi_compliance_guide` (FinCEN Small Entity Compliance Guide (Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting)), `fincen_amla_material` (FinCEN Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 Implementation Material), `frb_sr_letter` (Federal Reserve Supervision and Regulation (SR) / Consumer Affairs (CA) Letters), `occ_bulletin` (OCC Bulletins), `occ_interpretive_letter` (OCC Interpretive Letters), `fdic_fil` (FDIC Financial Institution Letters (FILs)), `cfpb_supervisory_guidance` (CFPB Supervisory Guidance), `cfpb_circular` (CFPB Consumer Financial Protection Circulars), `dfars_pgi` (DFARS PGI (Procedures, Guidance, and Information)), `ftc_advisory_opinion` (FTC Advisory Opinions), `ftc_policy_statement` (FTC Policy Statements (1967-present)), `ftc_hsr_interpretation` (FTC HSR Premerger Notification Interpretations: the Commission's formal interpretations under 16 C.F.R. 803.30 (1978-2000, a closed series) and the Premerger Notification Office's informal interpretations (1983-present; the publisher serves none from 1997)), `ftc_advocacy_filing` (FTC Advocacy Filings: comments and letters to state legislatures, state courts, governors and other federal agencies on the competition effects of a proposed measure (1985-present). Advisory only: they bind nobody and decide no case), `nlrb_gc_memo` (NLRB General Counsel Memoranda), `nlrb_advice_memo` (NLRB Division of Advice Memoranda (rolling 10-year window, not the full archive)), `cpsc_advisory_opinion` (CPSC Office of General Counsel Advisory Opinions (historical, 1970s-2012)), `cpsc_secg` (CPSC Small Entity Compliance Guides), `whd_opinion_letter` (DOL Wage and Hour Division Opinion, Ruling and Administrator Interpretation Letters (FLSA, FMLA, DBRA, SCA, CCPA, MSPA; 1993-present)), `whd_foh` (DOL Wage and Hour Field Operations Handbook (WHD internal enforcement procedure, not law; 22 chapters)), `bis_advisory_opinion` (BIS (Bureau of Industry and Security) Advisory Opinions), `ddtc_commodity_jurisdiction` (DDTC (Directorate of Defense Trade Controls) Commodity Jurisdiction Determinations), `ddtc_guidance` (DDTC (Directorate of Defense Trade Controls) Policy Guidance Documents), `ofac_faq` (OFAC (Office of Foreign Assets Control) Frequently Asked Questions), `hhs_ocr_hipaa_faq` (HHS Office for Civil Rights HIPAA FAQs), `hhs_ocr_hipaa_guidance` (HHS Office for Civil Rights HIPAA Guidance Materials), `hhs_ocr_resolution_agreement` (HHS Office for Civil Rights HIPAA Resolution Agreements and Civil Money Penalties), `fcc_declaratory_ruling` (FCC (Federal Communications Commission) Declaratory Rulings), `ferc_policy_statement` (FERC (Federal Energy Regulatory Commission) Policy Statements), `doe_appliance_guidance` (DOE Appliance Standards Guidance and FAQs), `eeoc_guidance` (EEOC (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission) Enforcement and Policy Guidance, including Compliance Manual sections), `irs_written_determination` (IRS Written Determinations under 26 U.S.C. § 6110: Private Letter Rulings (PLR), Technical Advice Memoranda (TAM) and Chief Counsel Advice (CCA). Each is directed only to the taxpayer who requested it and, by § 6110(k)(3), may not be used or cited as precedent).

`US_TAX_TREATY` sources: `us_tax_treaty` (U.S. Bilateral Income Tax Treaties), `us_tax_treaty_technical_explanation` (Treasury Technical Explanations (article-by-article commentary on a tax treaty)).

`US_TREATY` sources: `us_treaty` (Treaty and International Agreement Text (Stat., U.S.T., Bevans, FATCA agreements, free trade agreements)), `senate_treaty` (Senate Treaty Records (transmittal, parties and proceedings)), `senate_treaty_resolution` (Senate Resolutions of Advice and Consent, including the reservations, understandings and declarations that narrow a treaty's effect in US law), `senate_treaty_document` (Treaty Documents (CDOC TDOC series): the President's message transmitting a treaty to the Senate, with the instrument's text), `senate_executive_report` (Senate Executive Reports: the committee's report recommending advice and consent to a treaty, with its analysis of the instrument).

`STATE_AGENCY_GUIDANCE` sources: `state_insurance_bulletin` (State Department of Insurance Bulletins), `state_financial_bulletin` (State Financial-Institutions Regulator Bulletins (banking, credit unions, trust companies, escrow agents, consumer lenders, money transmitters; AZ and OR only, where that regulator shares an index with the insurance regulator)).

`AGENCY_ADJUDICATION` sources: `mspb_precedential` (MSPB Precedential Decisions), `mspb_nonprecedential` (MSPB Nonprecedential Orders), `olc_opinion` (DOJ Office of Legal Counsel Opinions (official bound volumes, 1933-2020)), `cfpb_enforcement_action` (CFPB Enforcement Actions), `sec_commission_opinion` (SEC Commission Opinions and Adjudicatory Orders), `bia_precedent` (BIA Precedent Decisions (I&N Dec.)), `ag_precedent` (Attorney General Immigration Decisions (I&N Dec.)), `immigration_admin_precedent` (INS and USCIS Administrative Precedent Decisions (I&N Dec.)), `nlrb_board_decision` (NLRB Board Decisions (1935 to date)), `ftc_administrative_decision` (FTC Part 3 Administrative Decisions). Every result carries its own `source`, so you can pass a hit's value straight back. An unrecognized value is rejected with 422.
source.title: Source

state.description: Jurisdiction filter. A 2-letter code for one of the 56 supported US jurisdictions (50 states + DC + PR, GU, VI, AS, MP), or `federal` to scope to USC / CFR / Constitution / federal rules. Pass a LIST to search several at once (`"state": ["ca", "ny", "tx"]`), which is one call instead of one per jurisdiction. Case-insensitive: `ca` and `CA` both work. An unrecognized value is rejected with 422 rather than silently matching nothing. Omit to search every jurisdiction.
state.title: State

titleNumber.description: Filter by USC/CFR title number (e.g., 17 for SEC, 42 for civil rights). Only meaningful for `USC`/`CFR`; ignored for state corpora whose titles are alphabetic (e.g. Texas `pe` = Penal Code).
titleNumber.title: Titlenumber

yearFrom.description: Only return sections dated in or after this year. Combine with `yearTo` for a window. A section matches on the first of three years it carries: the most recent amendment the publisher credits in its own history note; else its effective year, for a section adopted once and never amended; else, for corpora dated by publication rather than amendment (Federal Register proposed rules, agency guidance, adjudications, the treaty record), the document's own publication or issue year. Every one of those tracks the LAW or the document, never when we last rebuilt the corpus. A section carrying none of the three is excluded once either bound is set, so an unbounded search returns strictly more.
yearFrom.title: Yearfrom

yearTo.description: Only return sections dated in or before this year, on the same three years `yearFrom` describes. Note it filters the LAST such date, so a section amended in 2025 is excluded by `yearTo=2024` even though it existed in 2024. This is a currency filter, not point-in-time retrieval: the corpus holds one current text per citation.
yearTo.title: Yearto

bodyNote.description: Present only when `includeBody: true` was set and the bodies were withheld because the balance could not cover them (each row says `bodyNote: insufficient_credits`). The ranking was served and billed as usual; no body was charged.
bodyNote.title: Bodynote

changedSectionCount.description: Only present when `changedSince` is set: how many sections changed in that window, before ranking. Compare it against `count`. `changedSince` is a filter on a RANKED search, so a window holding more sections than one query can return is normal and the page you get is the most relevant slice of it, not all of it. When this number is larger than you can page to, the filter is a trigger rather than an inventory: subscribe to the board and poll `GET /watches/{id}/changes`, which is complete and costs no credits.
changedSectionCount.title: Changedsectioncount

citationMissReason.description: Present only when the whole query is a citation that did not resolve to a section, so the results are an ordinary search and not the section it names. `missReason` says why (`not_held`, `former_law`, `ambiguous_jurisdiction`, `out_of_scope_corpus`, `container_not_supported`), `missReasonHint` what to try, and `candidates` the held sections an ambiguous citation could mean. Absent for a question, for a citation that resolved, and when `citationOutsideFilters` already explains it. `malformed` is never reported here: a free-text question is not malformed. The same on every page of a query. No extra charge.

citationOutsideFilters.description: Your query is a citation to a real section that your filters exclude. To read it, retry without the filters named in `excludedBy`, or call `GET /us/statutes/resolve` without them. Null when the query is not a citation, when the citation is inside your filters (it then ranks first), or when it names no section we hold. `results` are unchanged: a filter is a promise, so the section is reported here and not forced into the results. The same on every page of a query.

count.description: How many results came back in THIS response, i.e. the length of `results`. It is not a total match count: the API ranks a bounded set of candidates rather than scoring the whole corpus, so no such total exists. Use `hasMore` to decide whether to ask for another page. With `matchType: "boolean"` the total is `totalMatches`.
count.title: Count

creditsConsumed.description: Credits actually charged for this call, after any refund. Failed work bills 0 and batch endpoints charge per item returned.
creditsConsumed.title: Creditsconsumed

droppedCount.description: Present only when this page is SHORT because that many ranked hits could not be loaded or serialized on our side and were left out: `count` is then smaller than the page the ranking chose. It is a fault, not a filter, and says nothing about whether those sections exist; repeat the call to get them. Absent on a complete page.
droppedCount.title: Droppedcount

hasMore.description: Whether more results exist beyond this page. For `any`, `all` and `phrase` this is relative to a bounded ranking pool of roughly 60 to 90 sections, so false means the pool is exhausted, not that nothing else in the corpus matches. Use `matchType: "boolean"` and follow `nextOffset` to page through every match.
hasMore.title: Hasmore

matchQuality.description: How strongly the evidence says result #1 answers the query. exact: a citation or section-number match. strong: the top result was correct about 94% of the time in our measurements (about 91% on questions whose answer is a statute or regulation). moderate: about 67%. weak: about 35%. none: nothing on point (same as noGoodMatch). Measured on our labelled evaluation set; tiers may be re-cut as the index changes, so treat unknown values as moderate. Null when `rankingDegraded` is true. The same on every page of a query.
matchQuality.title: Matchquality

nextOffset.description: Present only with `matchType` `boolean`, `all` or `phrase` while `hasMore` is true: the `offset` to send for the next page. Usually `offset` + `limit`. Past the relevance-ranked results a page can hold fewer rows than `limit` (candidates outside your filters, or failing the expression on full-text verification, are left out), and when verification runs out of time the page stops early and `nextOffset` resumes exactly where it stopped. Follow it rather than computing the offset. For `any` the field is absent: while `hasMore` is true, request the next page with `offset` + `limit`.
nextOffset.title: Nextoffset

noGoodMatch.description: True when nothing in the corpus looks on point for this query. It says nothing about whether the top result is the right section; check its citation and jurisdiction. False when the top result clears the relevance bar, or when the query is a citation or a section number that matched exactly. Null when `rankingDegraded` is true, because the bar is on the relevance model's scale. The same on every page of a query.
noGoodMatch.title: Nogoodmatch

notes.description: Plain-language notes about THIS page, present only when there is something to say: why an empty page was not charged and which filters emptied it, that `noGoodMatch` is charged, that a `changedSince` window of zero sections is not proof that nothing changed for a corpus without a captured change log, or that filters applied after the Boolean candidate index left the page shorter than `limit`.
examples: No sections matched your filters (state, corpusType). You were not charged.
notes.title: Notes

offset.description: The offset applied to this page.
offset.title: Offset

parsedQuery.description: Present only with `matchType: "boolean"`: the expression as it was read, in canonical form with explicit operators and grouping, e.g. `(work OR employment) AND retaliation`. Paste it back to run the same search.
parsedQuery.title: Parsedquery

pinpointNote.description: Present only when the request set `includePinpoint: true` and no pinpoints were looked up for this page, with the reason: the relevance model was unavailable (`rankingDegraded`), the candidate pool was incomplete (so the results are a coarser answer), or the pinpoint step itself failed (`lookup_failed`). Retry shortly for the full one. The pinpoint lookup is never charged on its own; a page served with `rankingDegraded: true` is refunded whether or not pinpoints were asked for (see `notes` and `creditsConsumed`), and any other page is charged as an ordinary search.
pinpointNote.title: Pinpointnote

pinpoints.description: Present only when the request set `includePinpoint: true`. Names the subsection each hit matched, keyed by the hit's `actId`: a hit for `30 mph urban district speed limit` reads `625 ILCS 5/11-601(c)(1)`. One entry per returned result, so a result with no entry here was not looked at (see `pinpointNote`). Read `located` first. When it is true, `pinpoint` and `citation` name the unit, `text` is its own text and `leadIn` the text of each ancestor it completes, and `charStart` / `charEnd` index into the `plain` text of `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}/body` (see `structure.textSha256`). When it is false, `reason` and `note` say why no subsection is named; the section itself is still a real match. A subsection is named only when the words of your query point at it: a question put in other words than the law's, or a query that fits several unrelated subsections equally, gets no pinpoint rather than a guess. `matchedTerms` shows which of your words the unit carries. No extra charge.

Why one `actId` missed, and what to send instead.

A bare id in `notFound` is ambiguous between the two things a caller most
needs to tell apart: an id they built by hand that never existed, and a real
section we do not hold. Read as the latter, the first one looks like missing
coverage, which is how a working integration gets abandoned.

reason.description: `assembled_id` -- this id does not exist, but the section does, under the ids in `didYouMean`. Almost always an id built from a citation: the chapter/article/part segments are not derivable from one, so take ids from a `/us/statutes/search` response instead. `unresolved_citation` -- the input is a citation and resolves to nothing we hold; check its form with `/us/statutes/resolve`. `not_in_corpus` -- nothing matching was found. Either the id is malformed beyond recovery, or the section is genuinely absent; check `/us/statutes/coverage` for the jurisdiction. `not_diagnosed` -- a miss past the first 20 in a batch; it was not looked into, so it carries no reason. Send it again in a smaller batch. `index_warming` -- the code this citation names is still being read: no verdict, not charged; retry after the `Retry-After` header. `state_session_law` -- the id starts `SSL_`: a state session law (an act as enacted), read at `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}`, not a code section.

scope.description:
Optional narrowing so this alert covers one citation instead of an entire source. Four mutually exclusive forms. Omit entirely to watch the whole source.

Hierarchy prefix: keys `title`, `chapter`, `part`, `section`, e.g. `{"title": "21", "part": "314"}` for 21 CFR part 314. Every level you set must match. `title` is required whenever any narrower level is set, and `section` also needs `chapter` or `part`. Sources without a title/chapter/part hierarchy return 400 (see `scopable` on `GET /boards`).

Exact section: `{"actId": "CFR_T21_P314_S314_50"}`, using the `actId` from search results and change events. Case-sensitive and validated at create time: an act_id we do not hold, or one from a different source, is a 400. Works on every source, and is the only way to follow a single Federal Register document.

Named source: `{"source": "fdic_fil"}`, for corpora that fold several independent bodies of law behind one `corpusType`. The `agency_guidance` board alone carries 47 named sources across 24 agencies, so an unscoped watch on it delivers FDIC letters, IRS notices, OFAC FAQs and DOE appliance standards together. Accepted on `agency_adjudication`, `agency_guidance`, `agency_manuals`, `cfr`, `federal_rules`; anything else returns 400. Pickable values are on the board's `sources` array in `GET /boards`.

Publishing agency: `{"agency": "irs"}`, covering every source that agency issues on the board (the IRS alone publishes 5 named series). Expanded when an event is matched, not when the watch is created, so a source registered later is covered automatically. Accepted on `agency_adjudication`, `agency_guidance`, `agency_manuals`; pickable values are on the board's `agencies` array in `GET /boards`.
scope.title: Scope

webhookAuth.description: Replace the outbound credential config. Sent as a whole object, not field by field: a scheme without a credential is not a partial edit, it is a broken config. Send `{"scheme": "none"}` to remove auth entirely. Keeping the same scheme and omitting `secret` retains the stored credential, so you can rename a header without re-entering the token.

When true, following every node and every `nextCursor` reaches every section the corpus holds; a level a jurisdiction does not record is not invented, so some codes list their sections directly beneath them. State court rules (`STATE_RULES`) are walked rule set first, then the containers each rule's record names inside its set. False for dated series such as the Federal Register and executive actions, and for corpora with no shared tree such as agency guidance. Every corpus is searchable either way; this only says whether you can NAVIGATE it instead of querying it.

It says nothing about how recently the corpus was refreshed, a different fact: a filtered corpus can be, and `FEDERAL_REGISTER_NOTICE` is, refreshed weekly. `GET /boards` answers that one.

One child division in a `GET /us/statutes/divisions` listing.

Interior nodes (titles, chapters, parts, codes, articles) carry a
`sectionCount` and `isLeaf: false`; drill into one by passing its
`identifier` back as the filter its `kind` names. Leaf nodes are sections and carry an `actId` you can pass to
`/us/statutes/section/{actId}`.

Pass it back as `subjectGroup`, with `titleNumber` and `part`, and it lists the same sections as the heading does. Null when the group has no single id: the same heading is two sibling groups in one part, or the id table is older than the heading. Omitted from the response when it has no value.

kind.description: `federal` for USC/CFR, `state` for the 50 states, `territory` for non-state jurisdictions (DC, Puerto Rico).
kind.title: Kind

sectionCount.description:
Distinct sections held for this jurisdiction, summed across its `corpora`. 0 means not yet covered.

One per provision or document, NOT per retrieval passage (see `totalPassages` for those). Repealed, transferred and reserved sections ARE counted: a legal research corpus serves them and a customer researching a historical question needs them. A SUPERSEDED prior version is not counted a second time when the section it supersedes is also served, because that is the same section twice -- but one with no current counterpart IS counted, since it is the only text we hold for that provision. Read `statusBreakdown` to see the split.
sectionCount.title: Sectioncount

sessionLaws.description: State session laws (acts as enacted) held for this jurisdiction, by legislative session, with each session's coverage status (`complete` or `partial`), how many laws we serve, withhold or know without text, the expected total (`denominator`), `openGaps` and when it was `measuredAt`. Beside the sessions it carries the `series` and `instrumentTypes` that exist (the values `GET /us/session-laws/list` accepts) and the span of approval dates held (`earliestApprovedDate`, `latestApprovedDate`); each of those four is omitted when it cannot be read. A separate corpus: read and list the laws with `/us/session-laws`, not `/us/statutes/search`, and resolve their citations with `/us/statutes/resolve`. The whole block is absent when we hold no session laws for the jurisdiction, and whenever session-law coverage cannot be read; absence is a gap in our collection, not a statement that the jurisdiction enacts none.

statusBreakdown.description:
Per-corpusType `act_status` split over the same sections `corpora` counts, e.g. `{"REGULATION": {"inForce": 12151, "repealed": 10640, "transferred": 5426}}`.

Published so a large section count can be read as maintained law plus retained history rather than as an undifferentiated total: Montana holds 28,217 regulation sections of which 12,151 are in force, and without this split that reads either as 28,217 current rules or as a coverage problem, and it is neither.

⚠️ `inForce` is what the ingester recorded, and it is NOT a complete census of current law: a zero means the status was never determined, never that the corpus is entirely inoperative. It is the status recorded for the section; the currency verdict is `goodLawStatus` on each section, which is `unknown` where a jurisdiction does not publish repeal information. The `unknown` key counts sections whose status is not stated. Absent when a jurisdiction has not been measured exactly.
statusBreakdown.title: Statusbreakdown

nextCursor.description:
Opaque token to resume this listing. Always present: null unless `truncated` is true. Treat it as opaque: it encodes a storage position, and building one by hand will not work.

Ordering. A cursor starting `o~` continues one listing in a single statutory order, so concatenating its pages gives the sorted whole. A cursor starting `s~` walks a container too large to sort in one pass: each page is in statutory order, pages follow storage order, and the union of every page is the complete container, so sort it yourself once you hold it all.

WebhookAuthRequest.description:
How a delivery should authenticate itself to your endpoint.

SEPARATE FROM `webhookSecret`, and the distinction is the point.

info.description:
Public API for legal statutes and legislation.

**Authentication**: Pass your API key as `Authorization: Bearer vq_key_...` (preferred) or in the `X-API-Key` header. Sending two different keys in one request is rejected with a 401.

**Credits**: Each call costs API credits. See `GET /api/v1/api-credits/pricing` for the full pricing matrix.

## Jurisdictions

| Jurisdiction | Coverage | `countryCode` |
|---|---|---|
| **United States** | USC and the Statutes at Large, the CFR and its annual editions, all 56 state and territory statutory codes (50 states, DC and five territories), state administrative regulations, court rules, federal and state constitutions, federal agency guidance and adjudications, the Federal Register, the Sentencing Guidelines and US tax treaties. | `US` |

See the full [Coverage page](https://www.vaquill.ai/docs/api-guide/coverage) for the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction breakdown, or call `/us/statutes/coverage` for live counts. Coverage is per (jurisdiction, corpusType) pair, so treat that endpoint as the authoritative list rather than this summary.

## Endpoints

- **US Statutes**: Search and retrieve any of the corpora above with full text, resolve a citation to its exact section, browse the statutory hierarchy, read a section as it stood on a past date, and follow its change history, cross-references and defined terms
- **Board Watches**: Subscribe to a corpus source and get a webhook or email when it refreshes with real changes (free, API key required)
- **Pricing**: Credit costs per endpoint (no auth required)

## Rate limits

Limits are enforced per API key and scale with your plan. A `429` response includes a `Retry-After` header.

| Plan | Per minute | Per hour | Per day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vaquill API Pro | 60 | 1,000 | 2,000 |
| Vaquill API Business | 150 | 2,500 | 10,000 |

For full documentation, visit the [API Reference](https://www.vaquill.ai/docs/api-reference/).

post.description:
Read up to 50 state session laws in one call: the same record
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` returns, for each id or citation in `ids`, in the order you
sent them. Use it to enrich a list (ids from `/us/session-laws/list` or `/us/session-laws/changes`,
or a memo with a dozen session-law citations) without a round trip per law. To identify a citation
without reading the law, `POST /us/statutes/resolve` costs 2 credits per item and answers with
a `sessionLaw` match block (title, dates, source link). This route returns the full record and,
optionally, the first page of the text. It also helps under the default limit of 30 requests per
minute per key (a plan raises it).

**Cost**: 2 credits per law served, the single-lookup price. Batching saves round trips,
not credits. A miss is not charged, and `creditsConsumed` reports what was billed. A citation in
`ids` also pays the `/us/statutes/resolve` price (2 credits) as its own ledger line, as on
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}`: kept whenever we gave a verdict (a served law, an unresolved
or ambiguous citation), refunded when the session it points into is only partly collected or when we
failed. An id pays no resolve fee.

**Every entry gets an answer.** A served law is in `laws`; every other entry is in `notFound` with a
`status`, the finer `reason` the single route's 404 carries, the same `detail` sentence, and the
candidates where there are any. Every distinct entry is in `laws`, in `notFound`, or, when it names
a law an earlier entry already produced, in `resolved`, so a shorter `laws` array can always be
explained.

**Mapping your inputs.** `laws` holds only the laws served, so it cannot be zipped back onto `ids`
by position. Each law carries the `input` it answers, and `resolved` lists every input that did not
match an id exactly as sent (a citation, or an id cleaned of whitespace, quotes or a trailing
period) with the id it resolved to. Duplicates are collapsed first: an entry identical to an earlier
one after trimming is dropped, order is kept, and `deduped` says how many. Two different spellings of
one law (`S.F.No. 1552` and its `sessionLawId`) serve the law once, under the first, bill it once,
and list both in `resolved`.

| `status` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `resolved` | Served. |
| `not_held` | Served as a record: the registry knows the law and holds no text (`textStatus: not_held`). |
| `not_found` | No law carries the id. |
| `unparsed` | Reads as a citation no state session law we hold carries. |
| `ambiguous` | The citation names several laws, all in `didYouMean`, none chosen (Minnesota 2025 has two Chapter 1s). |
| `needs_jurisdiction` | A citation form several states share, naming none: send `jurisdiction`. |
| `session_not_fully_collected` | Nothing matched in a session we have only partly collected, so the law may exist. Not charged, resolve price included. |
| `federal` | Federal acts are read at `/us/statutes/section`. |
| `error` | We failed to look this entry up. Says nothing about the law, is refunded in full, and is safe to resend. |

`jurisdiction` scopes how every citation in the batch is read, as on the single route. It is
validated before anything is charged: a bad code is a 422.

`includeBody` adds the first page of each served law's text (about 30,000 characters) as
`body`, at the body price (6 credits) per law whose page is served, charged after the work
because the count is not knowable up front. It multiplies with the batch: 50 laws at
2 + 6 is 400 credits in one call. A law whose text is withheld, not held or
empty returns `body: null` and is not charged for it. If your balance cannot cover the pages after
the records were served, the records are returned without bodies rather than taking the paid-for
result away. `bodyNextCursor` continues a longer act on `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}/body`.

**Limits.** At most 50 distinct entries after duplicates collapse (a raw list of up to 200
is accepted so a run of repeats is not refused), each at most 300 characters. An empty list,
an over-long entry, more than 50 distinct entries or a bad `jurisdiction` is a 422 and is not
charged. At most 8 lookups run at once inside a call.

**Example**

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/batch" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"ids": ["SSL_MN_2025R_G_Y2025_C1", "S.F.No. 1552"], "jurisdiction": "mn"}'
```

```javascript
const res = await fetch("https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/batch", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ ids: ["SSL_MN_2025R_G_Y2025_C1", "S.F.No. 1552"], jurisdiction: "mn" }),
});
const { laws, notFound, resolved } = await res.json();
const byInput = new Map(laws.map((law) => [law.input, law]));
```

get.description:
A sync feed of the registry: every state law that began to be served, had its text added, was
corrected, unserved, withdrawn or merged, oldest first, as a cursor over an integer `id`. Poll it to
keep a copy of the registry current without re-listing it: read from `sinceId=0` once, then call
again with the `cursor` you were given. It covers state session laws only; federal acts (`SAL_...`)
are not in it.

**Cost**: 1 credit per page of up to 200 entries (default 50). An empty page is
an answer, "nothing changed since your cursor", and is charged. A request that fails validation
(422) is not charged; a failure on our side (500, 503) is refunded.

**Walking the feed.** Send `sinceId=0` for the first page. While `hasMore` is true, call again with
`sinceId` set to `cursor`: `id` only grows and a page carries the entries after `sinceId` and
nothing else, so no entry is skipped or repeated between your calls. When `hasMore` is false you
have caught up as of this call; keep your cursor and ask again later. An empty page has
`cursor: null`: keep the one you hold. `id` is assigned in order, but a row can become visible
slightly after a later one if two writers commit at once (writers commit whole batches together, so
this has not happened); a job that cannot miss an entry can re-read the last few hundred ids.

**What an entry says.** `kind` is what happened (see its description), `sessionLawId` the law,
`jurisdiction` its state, and `detectedAt` when we recorded it: an upper bound on when the law
changed in the world, not an approval or effective date. Read the law at
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}`, or many at once with `POST /us/session-laws/batch`. A
`withdrawn` or `merged` entry is a tombstone: the law no longer answers there, and a `merged` entry
carries `mergedInto`, the `sessionLawId` to read instead.

**Filter.** `jurisdiction` limits the feed to one state, `dc` or `pr`, and then `hasMore` means more
matching entries follow. The response echoes the applied filter as `jurisdiction` (null when
unfiltered); an empty `jurisdiction=` is a 422, not "every state". The cursor is a position in the
whole feed, so the same `sinceId` means the same point with or without the filter, and a filtered
page can skip ids.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/changes?sinceId=0&limit=100" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

```javascript
let cursor = 0;
for (;;) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/changes?sinceId=${cursor}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}` },
  });
  const page = await res.json();
  for (const change of page.changes) handle(change);
  if (page.cursor !== null) cursor = page.cursor;
  if (!page.hasMore) break;
}
```

**Related endpoints**

- `GET /us/session-laws/list` lists the laws of one state, filtered; this feed is how you learn
  that one changed.
- `POST /us/session-laws/batch` reads many laws at once from the ids this feed returns.
- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` says which sessions we hold and how complete each is, in each
  jurisdiction's `sessionLaws` block.

**Nulls.** Every response field is present: one with no value is `null` (`[]` for a list). The
examples here leave the nulls out.

get.description:
List the session laws of one state: every act its legislature enacted, filtered by session,
approval date or effective date. Use it to ask "what became law in Texas this session" or "what
takes effect on September 1, 2025", and to collect the `sessionLawId`s the get and body endpoints
take. A session law is the act as enacted, before it is folded into a code; v1 serves state acts.

**Cost**: 1 credit per page of up to 200 rows (default 50), however
many rows the page holds. An empty page is an answer and is charged when it means nothing matches
your filters (see Empty pages). A request that fails validation (422) is not charged; a failure on
our side (500, 503) is refunded.

**Common questions.** `jurisdiction` is required and scopes everything; the other filters combine
with AND, and each parameter documents its own rules.

| Question | Filter | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Everything from one session | `session` | `session=2025R` |
| Approved in a window | `approvedFrom`, `approvedTo` | `approvedFrom=2025-04-01&approvedTo=2025-04-30` |
| Taking effect in a window or on one day | `effectiveFrom`, `effectiveTo` (laws whose first-to-last effective dates overlap the window; one day: the same date in both) | `effectiveFrom=2025-09-01&effectiveTo=2025-09-01` |
| Vetoed measures, or what did not become law | `isLaw`, `enactmentOutcome` (repeatable) | `isLaw=false&enactmentOutcome=vetoed` |
| Laws whose text can be read | `hasText`, `textStatus` | `hasText=true` |
| What changed since my last sync | `updatedSince` | `updatedSince=2026-10-01` |
| Find by words in the title or printed bill number | `q` | `q=court fees` |
| Narrow by numbering series or kind of measure | `series`, `instrumentType` | `series=general` |

A malformed value, or a range whose end precedes its start, is a 422. A well-formed value that
matches nothing (an unknown `session`, a date range with no laws) is a 200 with `results: []`.
Dates are `YYYY-MM-DD`. Read `effectiveFirst` and `effectiveLast` on each row and `effectiveDates`
on the law for the dates themselves. A date filter the data cannot satisfy for the state or session
(no law carries that kind of date) answers an empty page with `coverage.status: filter_unavailable`
naming `unavailableFilters`, not charged.

**Empty pages.** A page with no rows carries `coverage`, what we hold of the session you named (or
of the state, when you named none), so you can tell "nothing matches" from "we have not collected
this".

| `coverage.status` | Meaning | Charged |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `complete` | We hold every law the publisher lists: a true negative. | Yes |
| `partial` | The collection stopped short, so the law you want may exist. | No (`creditsConsumed` 0) |
| `not_held` | We hold nothing of it. | No (`creditsConsumed` 0) |

A request that names only the state, where some held sessions are complete and some partial, is
charged (for the complete ones it is a true negative), and `coverage.partialSessions` names the
sessions to doubt: send one as `session` to ask about it alone. If coverage cannot be read the page
is charged and `coverage` is omitted.

**Paging.** Rows come in `session.code` order, then `sessionLawId`, both as TEXT in the database's
collation, not in chapter order: `..._C10` sorts before `..._C2`, and the id's series and
numbering-year segments sort before the chapter. Sort client-side by `number` if you need chapter
order. The order is the same on every page and for every filter, and `order=desc` reverses it
exactly. Send `nextCursor` back as `cursor`, with the same filters, while `hasMore` is true (a
cursor sent with different filters is a 422, `cursor_query_mismatch`: restart without it). The
cursor is a keyset (it names the last row you saw), so laws added between your calls never repeat
or skip a row you have passed. `count` is the size of this page, not a total.

**Text.** Rows include laws whose text we do not hold (`textStatus: not_held`) or hold and withhold
(`withheld`, with `withheldReason`): the row is still a real law. A row is the summary only: the
full dates, sources and code sections are on `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}`. Each row
carries `charCount` and `estimatedBodyPages`, so you can price reading a law before you open it,
`citableAs` (the law cited as a lawyer writes it, `Minn. Laws 2025, ch. 1`) and `licenseNote` (what
its licence class permits).

**Cost of reading a law.** Reading a whole law costs `estimatedBodyPages` times the price
of one body page (6 credits). `estimatedBodyPages` is on the record next to `charCount`
and is the most pages the text can take: a page holds up to 30,000 characters and is cut
back to a paragraph break, so a long act usually takes fewer. It is null when the text cannot be
read (it can be when served, or when withheld for a reason we label and `/body` reads with
`includeUnverified`). Most acts take a page or two. Each body response carries `pagePrice` and
`estimatedRemainingCredits`, so you can stop whenever you have enough.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/list?jurisdiction=tx&effectiveFrom=2025-09-01&effectiveTo=2025-09-01&limit=25" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"

# only what changed since your last sync, and only measures that did not become law
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/list?jurisdiction=mn&updatedSince=2026-10-01&isLaw=false&enactmentOutcome=vetoed" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

```javascript
const url = new URL("https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/list");
url.search = new URLSearchParams({ jurisdiction: "mn", session: "2025R" });
const res = await fetch(url, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}` },
});
const { results, nextCursor, hasMore } = await res.json();
```

**Related endpoints**

- `GET /us/statutes/resolve` answers a citation that names a state session law rather than a
  code section with a `sessionLaw` block (`matched`, or `ambiguous` with every candidate),
  pointing here. It never changes `resolved` or `section`.
- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` lists, per jurisdiction under `sessionLaws`, the sessions held and
  whether each is `complete` or `partial`. A law missing from a `partial` session may still exist.
- Federal session laws (the Statutes at Large, `SAL_` ids) are read with
  `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}`, not here.

**Nulls.** Every response field is present: one with no value is `null` (`[]` for a list). The
examples here leave the nulls out. `publisher`, `provenance` and `session.coverageStatus` on a law,
and `coverage` on a list page with rows, are absent when they do not apply.

**Rate limits.** Calls count against your key's per-minute budget like every Data API route; a 429
carries `Retry-After`.

post.description:
Find state session laws by what they say. Send a question in plain words, words from a title, a quoted
phrase, a citation (`63-3004`), a code section or a bill number (`S.F.No. 1552`). You get the laws, best
first, each with the passage of its text that matched and a snippet around your words.

**Cost**: 4 credits per page, each page a new search. An empty result from a search narrowed by
`jurisdiction`, `session`, `series`, `instrumentType` or the approval dates is refunded and carries a `note`
naming the filters; an empty result with no filter is an answer ("nothing matches"), is charged, and carries
a `note`. A request that fails validation (422) is not charged, including a `query` with nothing to search
for (`??`, `the of`); a failure on our side (500, 503) is refunded. To read a law you found, use
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` (record) or its `/body` (text), which are priced on their own.

**What is searched.** The enacted text: the law as it reads once the act takes effect. Language an act
strikes out is not searched and does not appear in a snippet, so a repealed word cannot match as if it were
law. Only laws we serve with text are searched (see `GET /us/statutes/coverage`, `sessionLaws`, for what
each state holds). Laws whose text we withhold are returned only with `includeUnverified`, which also changes
how they are matched (see that parameter). `session` limits every kind of match to that session.

**How it ranks.** Keyword relevance (BM25), not meaning. Words are matched as written and stemmed
(`licensing` finds `licensed`), so a question has to share vocabulary with the act:
`teeth cleaning professional` does not find an act that says `dental hygienist`. A law matched by its
title AND its text, or by an exact part of your query, ranks above one matched a single way, whatever
the age of either. Among laws matched alike, the newer act comes first and an act that amends few code
sections comes before an omnibus one. Quote a phrase to require it verbatim. The act's own citation
(`Laws 2025, ch. 127`) is searched too.

**What a result says about itself.** `matchType` is `exact` when a quoted phrase, citation, code
section or bill number you typed matched, otherwise `text`; `matchedBy` lists every way. Neither says
the law is the right one: a question with no true answer still returns its closest words, and there is no
"no good match" flag because keyword scores do not separate the two cases. Read the snippet.

**Paging.** `limit` is 1 to 25. `offset` plus `limit` reaches at most the 60 best matches; narrow with
`jurisdiction`, `session`, `series`, `instrumentType` or the approval dates rather than paging deeper.

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/search" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer vq_key_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "can the sheriff pay with a debit card", "jurisdiction": "al", "limit": 5}'
```

```javascript
const res = await fetch("https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/search", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { Authorization: "Bearer vq_key_...", "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ query: '"credit card or debit card"', jurisdiction: "al", limit: 5 }),
});
const { results } = await res.json();
```

**Related.** `GET /us/session-laws/list` filters one state's laws by session, series and date;
`POST /us/session-laws/batch` reads up to 50 laws by id; `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}/enactments`
lists the acts a publisher's own tables tie to a code section.

get.description:
Everything we hold about one state session law except its text: identity and citation, session,
approval date, every printed effective date (`effectiveDates`, always a list), other printed dates,
the code sections the publisher's own table lists the act as affecting (`codeSectionsAffected`),
its sources with hashes, and whether its text is held. Fetch the text, paged, from
`/us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}/body`.

**Cost**: 2 credits. A citation sent in place of the id adds the `/us/statutes/resolve`
price (2 credits), kept whenever we gave a verdict on the citation (a served law, an
unresolved or ambiguous citation), so `creditsConsumed` is then 4 when the law is
served. The fee is refunded when the session the citation points into is only partly collected,
when the text is not a state session-law citation at all (the 404 lists the accepted forms), and on
a failure on our side (500, 503). A 404 does not keep this route's own price, and a 422 is not
charged.

**Id or citation.** Send a `sessionLawId` from a list result, or a citation or bill number
(`S.F.No. 1552`); the `sessionLawId` path parameter says which forms are matched. `resolvedFrom`
tells you what your input matched and the `sessionLawId` to send next time. Prefer the id: it has no
resolve fee and is unambiguous. A citation matching several laws is a 404 with
`reason: ambiguous_citation` and every candidate in `didYouMean`. A citation that names no state
(`Laws 2025, ch. 1`) takes the optional `jurisdiction` (`mn`), which supplies the state and rejects
a conflicting one; it has no effect on an id.

**Fields worth knowing**

- `citableAs` is the law as a lawyer cites it (`Minn. Laws 2025, ch. 1`) and `citationShort` a
  compact label (`MN ch. 1 (2025)`); each is null where we do not know the state's form. Where a
  special session restarts the numbering, `citableAs` is the conventional reading of the first law,
  so the citation is an `ambiguous_citation` 404 that marks this one `defaultSessionLawId`.
- `sourceUrl` is the official page the text was collected from, on a government host, present on a
  withheld law too. `licenseNote` says what the law's licence class permits.
- `approvedDate` is when the act was signed, not an effective date. Where the registry holds none
  but the publisher dates the governor's signature among its other milestones, we fill it from that
  label and set `approvedDateDerived: true`; a presented or passed date is not read as an approval.
  The list's `approvedFrom` and `approvedTo` match a derived date too.
- `effectiveDates` holds the dates the publisher prints as effective. It is empty when none is
  printed or the date is printed as a rule ("the day following final enactment"), which does not
  mean the act is not in force. `otherDates` holds the rest (approval, filing, presentment), each
  with its `kind`.
- `codeSectionsAffected` is the publisher's table as printed, empty when it prints none (`title`
  usually names the sections in prose).
- `publisher` carries what the publisher states about the act: `publisherFields` (its own fields
  verbatim; keys differ by state and nothing is normalised), `publisherIds`, `otherCitations`,
  `legislatureNumber`, `sessionLastYear`, `printedPageStart`, `printedPageEnd` and
  `documentKindAsPrinted`. `provenance` says how the text was obtained (`textMethod`,
  `pagesWithText`, the bound `volume`) and lists the collector's own `caveats`.
  `session.coverageStatus` says whether we hold the whole session (`complete`) or part of it
  (`partial`, so a missing neighbour may exist). These three are absent, not null, if they cannot
  be read; the price is the same.
- `textStatus: withheld` with a `withheldReason` means the law is returned in full and only its
  text is held back (`/body` answers `available: false`, free). Check `amendatoryMarkup` before
  quoting an amending act: where it is `lost`, deleted words can read as law.

**Cost of reading a law.** Reading a whole law costs `estimatedBodyPages` times the price
of one body page (6 credits). `estimatedBodyPages` is on the record next to `charCount`
and is the most pages the text can take: a page holds up to 30,000 characters and is cut
back to a paragraph break, so a long act usually takes fewer. It is null when the text cannot be
read (it can be when served, or when withheld for a reason we label and `/body` reads with
`includeUnverified`). Most acts take a page or two. Each body response carries `pagePrice` and
`estimatedRemainingCredits`, so you can stop whenever you have enough.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025R_G_Y2025_C1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"

# by bill number (URL-encode the citation), or a citation that names no state scoped to one
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/S.F.No.%201552" -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/Laws%202025,%20ch.%201?jurisdiction=mn" -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

```javascript
const id = "SSL_MN_2025R_G_Y2025_C1";
const res = await fetch(`https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}` },
});
const law = await res.json();
```

**Related endpoints**

- `GET /us/statutes/resolve` answers a citation that names a state session law rather than a
  code section with a `sessionLaw` block (`matched`, or `ambiguous` with every candidate),
  pointing here. It never changes `resolved` or `section`.
- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` lists, per jurisdiction under `sessionLaws`, the sessions held and
  whether each is `complete` or `partial`. A law missing from a `partial` session may still exist.
- Federal session laws (the Statutes at Large, `SAL_` ids) are read with
  `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}`, not here.

**Nulls.** Every response field is present: one with no value is `null` (`[]` for a list). The
examples here leave the nulls out. `publisher`, `provenance` and `session.coverageStatus` on a law,
and `coverage` on a list page with rows, are absent when they do not apply.

**Rate limits.** Calls count against your key's per-minute budget like every Data API route; a 429
carries `Retry-After`.

get.description:
The act's text exactly as printed, one page of about 30,000 characters at a
time, cut at a paragraph break where one is near. Follow `nextCursor` while
`hasMore` is true; `pageStart` / `pageEnd` / `totalChars` are character offsets
into the whole text, and concatenating the pages in order reproduces it.

**Cost**: 6 credits per page served; each page is charged on its own, so you can stop
whenever you have enough. `pagePrice` is what this page cost, `totalPages` the estimated pages in
all, and `estimatedRemainingCredits` the pages still to come times the price.

**Cost of reading a law.** Reading a whole law costs `estimatedBodyPages` times the price
of one body page (6 credits). `estimatedBodyPages` is on the record next to `charCount`
and is the most pages the text can take: a page holds up to 30,000 characters and is cut
back to a paragraph break, so a long act usually takes fewer. It is null when the text cannot be
read (it can be when served, or when withheld for a reason we label and `/body` reads with
`includeUnverified`). Most acts take a page or two. Each body response carries `pagePrice` and
`estimatedRemainingCredits`, so you can stop whenever you have enough.


Worked example: the longest act we hold, Ohio's 2025 budget act (HB 96, 9,571,132
characters), takes at most 399 pages, 2,394 credits to read in full.

**Where a page starts.** Follow `nextCursor` from the page before, or send `startChar`, a
character offset into the text (0-based, the scale of `pageStart` and `totalChars`), to jump to a
place you know. Send one or the other, never both (a 422, uncharged). A `startChar` page costs and
sizes the same as any other. `startChar` has no version binding of its own, so add
`expectTextSha256` (the `textSha256` you read the text under): if the text was re-collected since,
the answer is a 409 and nothing is charged. There is no page-size parameter: a page is always about
30,000 characters, so its price is fixed.

**Attribution.** Every outcome carries `citation`, `jurisdiction`, `session`, `approvedDate` and
`sourceUrl` (the official copy on a government host, present when the text is withheld or not held
too), so a page is attributable on its own.

**Id only.** This route takes a `sessionLawId`, not a citation: resolve a citation once with
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` and use the id it returns.

**Not served, not charged.** When we do not serve the text (`textStatus` is not `held`), the answer
is a 200 with `available: false`, a `reason` (`not_held`, `withheld`, `pending` or `empty_text`),
`creditsConsumed: 0`, the `withheldReason` for a withheld law, and the official `sourceUrl`. A
federal id (`SAL_...`) is a 404 (`federal_session_law`); read federal session laws with
`GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}`. Errors (unknown id 404, stale cursor or mismatched
`expectTextSha256` 409, malformed cursor or `startChar` 422) are not charged, and a failure on our
side (500, 503) is refunded. The parameters and the 409 response give the exact conditions.

**Past versions: `version`.** We keep every version of a law's text that we served or adopted. List
them with `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}/versions`, then send one of those numbers as
`version`; omit it for the current version. The response then names `version` and
`isCurrentVersion`, and the page, `nextCursor` and `textSha256` belong to that version. The price is
unchanged: 6
credits per page, whichever version you read. A `version` the law does not have is a 404, refunded.
Without `version` and `includeUnverified` the response is the plain current-text page.

**Text we hold back: `includeUnverified`.** A law whose text has a defect we have not cleared is
`withheld`, and by default `/body` answers `available: false`, free. Send `includeUnverified=true`
to read its text when the reason it is held back is one we can label. The page then carries
`textReliability` (`unverified`: a check has not been completed, or `known_issue`: we have evidence
of the defect), a stable `reasonCode` and a one-sentence `notice` to show beside the text: the text
may show deleted (struck) or vetoed law as if it were enacted, so check the printed act at
`sourceUrl` before relying on it. The codes that serve the text, flagged, are `markup_unverified`,
`strike_unchecked`, `struck_text_shown_as_current`, `struck_text_merged`, `veto_unchecked` and
`licence_unconfirmed`. Some text is not served even when you opt in, and answers
`available: false`, free, with the `reasonCode` and no text: a law whose licence bars use
(`licence_barred`), text that failed our own validation (`validation_failed`), a session we cannot
yet tell apart from another (`session_unresolved`), a source we have not yet audited
(`collector_unaudited`) and a reason we have not classified (`unclassified`). A served law with
`includeUnverified=true` reads as usual and says `textReliability: verified`. Such a page costs
6 credits like any other and can be combined with `version`. The fields `version`,
`isCurrentVersion`, `textReliability`, `reasonCode` and `notice` are omitted unless you asked for them.

**Amendatory markup.** An amending act prints the language it deletes and inserts. Where
`amendatoryMarkup` is `preserved`, that markup is in `text` in the convention `markupConvention`
names: `wdiff` writes deleted language `[-like this-]` and inserted language `{+like this+}`;
`publisher_literal` keeps the publisher's own markers as printed (Minnesota's `new text begin` and
`deleted text begin`); `mixed` has both. Where it is `lost`, the publisher printed markup our text
does not keep, so deleted words can read as law: check the source before quoting. Only the as-printed
text is served; there is no clean "as enacted" view.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/body" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"

# jump to a character offset, pinned to the version of the text you read
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/body?startChar=29987&expectTextSha256=02693d5b55d4709b" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"

# an older version (list the versions first at .../versions), or a withheld law's labelled text
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/body?version=1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_LA_2025R_G_C2/body?includeUnverified=true" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

```javascript
const MY_BUDGET = 100; // the most you will spend to finish reading, in credits
let cursor;
let text = "";
do {
  const url = new URL("https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/body");
  if (cursor) url.searchParams.set("cursor", cursor);
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}` },
  });
  const page = await res.json();
  if (!page.available) break; // withheld or not held: page.sourceUrl is the official copy
  text += page.text;
  if (page.estimatedRemainingCredits > MY_BUDGET) break; // stop whenever you have enough
  cursor = page.nextCursor;
} while (cursor);
```

- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` lists, per jurisdiction under `sessionLaws`, the sessions held and
  whether each is `complete` or `partial`. A law missing from a `partial` session may still exist.
- Federal session laws (the Statutes at Large, `SAL_` ids) are read with

get.summary: Get a state session law's text, current or a past version

get.description:
Every version of one state session law that we served or adopted, newest first, and which of them is
current. A law's text can be corrected after we first serve it (a better extraction of the same
source, a re-collection), so the version you read yesterday may not be the one a plain call returns
today. This route lists each version with what identifies it (when we recorded it, its length, its
hash, how the text was taken) and how its text can be read. It carries no text: read one version with
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}/body?version=N`.

**Cost**: 1 credit per call, however many versions the law has. A law with a single version
answers a list of one and is charged: "this law has never changed" is the answer you paid for. Reading
a version's text is a separate call at the body price (6 credits per page), the same as the
current text. A request that fails validation (422) is never charged.
A law that is not found (404) is never charged.
A failure on our side (500, 503) is refunded.

**Edge cases.** A law that is in the registry but has no version row (its current version is not set,
or it was withdrawn or merged into another law) answers `200` with `versions: []`, `count: 0` and a
`note`, and is not charged; it is never the 404 "no law carries this id". One answer lists at most
100 versions, newest first; `truncated: true` says older versions exist that it does not show.

**Id only.** This route takes a `sessionLawId`, not a citation: resolve a citation once with
`GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` and use the id it returns. A federal id (`SAL_...`) is a 404
(`federal_session_law`), as on `/body`.

**What a version says.** `version` is the number to send as `version` on `/body`. Numbers can have
gaps: a version we recorded and never served or adopted is not listed. Exactly one listed version has
`isCurrent: true`, and `currentVersion` repeats its number: it is the text a plain `/body` call
serves. `recordedAt` dates our copy of the text, not the act (`approvedDate` on the law does that).
`totalChars` and `textSha256` identify the text: two versions with the same hash have the same text.
`citation`, `title` and `approvedDate` are as that version recorded them, so a correction that fixed
a title shows here.

| `textAccess` | Reading that version's text |
| --- | --- |
| `served` | A plain call to `/body?version=N`. |
| `includeUnverified` | The law is held back (`textStatus: withheld`); the text is readable only with `includeUnverified=true`, labelled by `textReliability` and `reasonCode` (it may show deleted or vetoed law as if it were enacted). |
| `none` | There is no text for this version, or the law's text may not be published (a licence that bars use, or text that failed our own validation). |

The law-level `textStatus`, `textReliability` and `reasonCode` are the same fields, with the same
meaning, as on `/body`. `textReliability` is omitted when no text of the law may be read, and
`reasonCode` when the law is served and verified. To check that nothing changed under you, compare
`textSha256` here with the one you read; the cursor rules for an older version are on `/body`.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/versions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"

# then read the first version's text, one page at the body price
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1/body?version=1" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

```javascript
const id = "SSL_MN_2025S1_G_Y2025_C1";
const res = await fetch(`https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/session-laws/${encodeURIComponent(id)}/versions`, {
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.VAQUILL_API_KEY}` },
});
const { versions, currentVersion } = await res.json();
const older = versions.filter((v) => !v.isCurrent && v.textAccess === "served");
```

**Related endpoints**

- `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}/body` reads the text of the current version, or of the one you
  name with `version`. It also takes `includeUnverified=true` for a law we hold back.
- `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` is the law's record (dates, sources, code sections affected,
  whether its text is held); it always describes the current version.
- `GET /us/session-laws/changes` is the registry's change feed: a `corrected` entry there is how you
  learn that a copy of a law you hold may be stale, and this route is where you see what changed.
- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` says which sessions we hold and how complete each is, under each
  jurisdiction's `sessionLaws` block.
- Federal session laws (the Statutes at Large, `SAL_` ids) are not served here. Read them with
  `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}`.

**Nulls.** A field of a version with no value (`citation`, `title`, `approvedDate`, `totalChars`,
`textSha256`, `textMethod`, `amendatoryMarkup`, `markupConvention`) is `null`. `textReliability` and
`reasonCode` on the law are absent, not null, when they do not apply. The examples here leave the
nulls out.

**Rate limits.** Calls count against your key's per-minute budget like every Data API route; a 429
carries `Retry-After`.
