post.description:
How many sections sit in a jurisdiction, corpus, code, title, chapter, part,
article or federal rule set. The scoping filters (`code`, `article`, `chapter`,
`part`) take the same values and pairing rules as on `/us/statutes/search`.

**Cost**: 1 credit. A scope that matches nothing is refunded, because an empty
answer here is usually a wrong filter rather than a finding.

Use it to size a job before you run it. Walking a container with
`/us/statutes/divisions` and hydrating what you find is cheap per call and adds
up across a whole corpus, so this is the call that tells you what you are about
to spend before you spend it.

**A natural-language `query` is refused, on purpose.** Search ranks it over a
bounded window, so "how many sections match this question" has no answer beyond
the size of that window. Without a `query` this counts a SCOPE, which is exact.
Pair the two: count the scope here, enumerate it with `/us/statutes/divisions`,
then rank within it using `/us/statutes/search`.

**Boolean counts.** With `matchType: "boolean"` and a terms-and-connectors
`query` (the syntax of `/us/statutes/search`), this counts the sections that
satisfy the expression within the scope, the same figure a Boolean search
reports as `totalMatches`. `isExact: false` marks an upper bound: the expression
uses an operator the index cannot judge exactly (phrases, `/s`, `/p`, proximity,
`atleastN`, wildcards inside proximity) or a filter it does not apply (anything
beyond `corpusType`, `state`, `actStatus` and `excludeRepealed`). Same price; a
malformed expression is a 422 and is not charged.

The figure counts SECTIONS. Long sections are stored as several passages and are
counted once.

**What an unscoped count leaves out.** With no `corpusType`, past editions
(annual CFR printings) and proposals (bills) are not counted, exactly as in
`/us/statutes/search` and `/us/statutes/coverage`; the echo lists them under
`excludedCategories`. Name one in `corpusType` to count it.

**Agreement with `/us/statutes/divisions`.** The browse counts distinct sections, so
a section re-ingested additively (a superseded and a current copy under one id) is
one section there. A scope of up to 4,000 sections is counted the same way
(`scope.countBasis` is `distinctActIds`), so the children's `sectionCount` values sum
to this figure. A larger scope reports `countBasis: "sectionPoints"` with
`scope.supersededSectionPoints`, the most such copies could overstate the figure by.

get.description:
Self-describing coverage matrix: a legend of every `corpusType` token (what it contains and whether it is federal or state-scoped) plus, for each jurisdiction, the ingested DOCUMENT counts per corpusType in `corpora` (one per section or document, not per retrieval passage; `totalPassages` is the passage count). Read a jurisdiction's `corpora` keys, then pass one as `corpusType` to `/us/statutes/search` (with `state` for state-scoped corpora). A corpusType absent from `corpora` is not held for that jurisdiction. A legend entry's `browsable` says whether `GET /us/statutes/divisions` can walk that corpus as a tree.

Congressional bills are not held; enacted federal text is under `SESSION_LAW` and `USC`. `FEDERAL_BILL` (proposed text, never law, outside every total) is registered and returns nothing today; `proposedCorpora` reports its count.

**Territories.** Beyond the 50 states and DC, five territories are jurisdictions of their own, each with `kind: territory`: Puerto Rico (`pr`), Guam (`gu`), the U.S. Virgin Islands (`vi`), American Samoa (`as`) and the Northern Mariana Islands (`mp`). All five hold statutes, regulations and court rules. Constitutions (`STATE_CONSTITUTION`) are held for `pr`, `as` and `mp` and not for `gu` or `vi`. Attorney general opinions (`STATE_AG_OPINION`) are held for `pr` and DC only, and a register (`STATE_REGISTER`) for `mp`. Puerto Rico statutes are held in Spanish, as enacted, and resolve by their `L.P.R.A.` number where that number is printed on the section; the LexisNexis annotated edition (English translation, annotations, index) is not held.

This reports what we hold, not how recently it was refreshed. For the age of a source call `GET /boards` (free): `lastRetrievedAt` and `cadence` record when we last CHECKED, not when the law last changed. Where a publisher states its own currency, that rides on each section as `currentThrough`.

**Free.** Requires an API key and is rate-limited, but costs no credits.

State session laws (acts as enacted) are at `/us/session-laws`. Where we hold any for a jurisdiction, its `sessionLaws` block lists its sessions (`complete` or `partial`), how many laws we serve and withhold (`withheldCount`, each with a stated reason), the expected total and open gaps, and the `series`, `instrumentTypes` and approval-date span that exist (the values `GET /us/session-laws/list` accepts). A jurisdiction with none has no block. This is the one place session-law coverage is served, so check it before you list.

get.description:
Walk the statutory tree one level at a time, in statutory order. Each call
returns the immediate children of wherever you are. Following every node down,
and every `nextCursor` across, reaches every section the corpus holds for that
scope, so a code can be enumerated without searching.

**Cost**: 1 credit per call. Refunded on a failure, and not charged at all on a request whose
filters do not fit the corpus (422), that names a container that does not exist, or that returns
no rows: the credit is taken only once a level with rows is ready to return.

Pass the deepest level you already know; the response returns the level below it:

- `corpusType=USC` -> the titles
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=42` -> the chapters in Title 42
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=18` -> the parts of Title 18 (a title whose chapters sit in parts, subtitles or divisions lists those first)
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=18&part=I` -> the chapters in Part I of Title 18
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=8&chapter=12` -> the subchapters of Chapter 12 (a chapter with no subchapters lists its sections)
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=8&chapter=12&subchapter=II` -> the parts of Subchapter II (Parts I to IX)
- `corpusType=USC&titleNumber=8&chapter=12&subchapter=II&part=I` -> the sections in Part I (leaf)
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=17` -> the chapters of Title 17 (a title with subtitles, such as 29, lists them first; a title whose parts sit in no chapter lists its parts)
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=29&subtitle=B` -> the chapters of Subtitle B of Title 29 (Subtitle A lists its parts directly)
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=29&chapter=XIV` -> the parts of Chapter XIV of Title 29
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=17&part=240` -> the subparts and subject groups of Part 240 (a part with neither lists its sections)
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=17&part=240&subpart=A` -> the subject groups of Subpart A
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=17&part=240&subpart=A&subjectGroup=Rules of General Application` -> the sections in that subject group (leaf)
- `corpusType=CFR&titleNumber=17&part=240&subjectGroup=ECFRf2ef38fa463cdfa` -> the same sections (leaf), by the group's eCFR id (a subject-group node's `subjectGroupId`)
- `corpusType=STATE&state=tx` -> the state's codes
- `corpusType=STATE&state=tx&code=tx_pe` -> the titles of the Texas Penal Code
- `corpusType=STATE&state=tx&code=tx_pe&title=5` -> the chapters in Title 5 of the Texas Penal Code
- `corpusType=STATE&state=tx&code=tx_gv&title=5&subtitle=B` -> the chapters in Subtitle B of Title 5 of the Texas Government Code
- `corpusType=STATE&state=ca&code=ca_pen` -> the parts of the California Penal Code
- `corpusType=STATE&state=ca&code=ca_edc&title=1&division=1&part=11&chapter=2` -> the articles of the Education Code's Chapter 2 in Part 11 (one of its many chapters numbered 2)
- `corpusType=STATE&state=ny&code=ny_jud&article=2` -> the sections in a New York article (leaf)
- `corpusType=STATE&state=il&code=il_225` -> the acts in 225 ILCS, a code that is a single chapter
- `corpusType=STATE&state=de&code=de_6&article=2` -> the parts of UCC Article 2 in Delaware Title 6, which sits outside any chapter
- `corpusType=STATE&state=de&code=de_6&article=2&part=2` -> the sections in Part 2 of UCC Article 2 (leaf)
- `corpusType=REGULATION&state=ny&code=ny_10&chapter=I` -> the parts in Chapter I of 10 NYCRR
- `corpusType=STATE_RULES&state=tx` -> the state's court rule sets (Rules of Civil Procedure, each county's local rules, ...)
- `corpusType=STATE_RULES&state=tx&code=HARRIS` -> the rule sets inside Harris County's local rules, as `kind: chapter`
- `corpusType=STATE_RULES&state=wi&code=SCR61` -> the rules of Wisconsin SCR Chapter 61, which records no level inside it (leaf)
- `corpusType=CONSTITUTION` -> the articles and amendments of the US Constitution
- `corpusType=CONSTITUTION&article=Article III` -> the sections of Article III (leaf)
- `corpusType=STATE_CONSTITUTION&state=nm` -> the articles of the New Mexico Constitution
- `corpusType=FEDERAL_RULES` -> the rule sets (FRCP, FRE, FRCrP, ...)
- `corpusType=FEDERAL_RULES&code=frcp` -> the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (leaf)

Interior nodes carry a `sectionCount` and `isLeaf: false`; drill into one by passing its
`identifier` back as the filter its `kind` names (`title` is `titleNumber` on the U.S. Code and
CFR; `chapter`, `subchapter`, `part`, `subpart`, `subtitle`, `division`, `subdivision`,
`subjectGroup`, `code`, `article`, `act`, and on state regulations `umbrella`, `agency`,
`program`), keeping the filters you already passed. A listing can mix kinds, so read `kind` on
each node rather than assuming it from `level`. Leaf nodes are sections and carry an `actId` for
`/us/statutes/section/{actId}`.

Levels do not sit at a fixed depth. Pass each level a listing returned, in any order; a number
that fits more than one place (`part=I` in a chapter whose subchapters each have a Part I) is
refused with the containers to add. A state level is listed only where the corpus records it, so
which levels a code has is read from its own sections, and `note` says when a code records none
below the code. A number that repeats inside one code (a California chapter `2` sits in dozens of
parts) names one container only together with the levels above it; passed alone it lists the
sections of every container that carries it, flat, with a `note`. A state subtitle or division is
never matched across titles: pass the `title` it sits in. A CFR subject group has no stable
number, so its `identifier` is its heading, matched case-insensitively. Court rules
(`STATE_RULES`) list a state's rule sets first, as `kind: code`, then each container their rules
name, whatever the publisher calls the level, with the publisher's heading as `name`.

A listing larger than one response pages: `truncated` is true and `nextCursor` continues it. Pass
the cursor back with the same filters until it comes back null. If `note` says a listing could
not hold everything, it also says where the rest is.

Browse supports `USC`, `CFR`, `STATE`, `REGULATION`, `STATE_RULES`, `CONSTITUTION`,
`STATE_CONSTITUTION` and `FEDERAL_RULES`, which is also what `browsable` says on each
`GET /us/statutes/coverage` legend entry. The rest are dated series or share no tree: use
`/us/statutes/search` for those. Federal rules are published twice, by the Judicial Conference
(`frcp`, `fre`, ...) and as an appendix to the U.S. Code (`uscapp_t28a_fre`, ...); each is its own
rule set here, so neither is listed twice under one heading.

post.description:
Read a block of text (a brief, a memo, a model's answer) and return every distinct non-case legal
citation in it, each resolved to the section it names. The text-in counterpart of
`POST /us/statutes/resolve`: one call instead of extracting the citations yourself and sending them
in batches of 50. The text is never stored.

Extraction reads statutes, regulations, court rules, constitutions and registers, in federal and
state form (`42 U.S.C. § 1983(b)`, `Cal. Civ. Code § 1942`, `Fed. R. Civ. P. 12`, `8 CCR 1206-2`,
`N.Y. Const. art. I, § 8`); it does not extract case citations. It is measured, not perfect (about
0.92 to 0.98 precision and 0.80 to 0.85 recall on unseen opinion text), so a citation can be missed
and a non-citation read as one; `resolved` is what we verified. The same text can yield different
citations when `extractorVersion` changes. Pass `state` (the document's jurisdiction) so a citation
that names none, such as `Civil Rule 56.1`, is checked against the right one.

**Cost**: 2 credits per distinct citation (section, not pinpoint) sent to the resolver, the
same as `POST /us/statutes/resolve`. The extraction itself is free: `resolve: false` returns the
citations found and charges nothing. An unresolved citation is charged (the verdict is the
product); a session-law citation (`skipped: session_law`, read it under `/us/session-laws`) is not
resolved here and not charged. A citation we fail to process is refunded one by one, and an outage
that takes half of them or more answers 503 and refunds the call. The charge is taken after
extraction and before any lookup, so `creditsConsumed` is known up front. One call resolves at
most 200 distinct citations, so at most 400 credits; `truncated: true` says
more were found and only the listed ones were charged.

**Limits.** `text` is at most 200,000 characters (a 422, never a truncation). A key may send
5,000 resolutions a day through this route; past that the
call answers 429 with `Retry-After` and nothing is charged.

**Rows.** `raw` is the first mention copied exactly from your text and `charStart` / `charEnd` its
offsets (`text[charStart:charEnd] == raw`, in Unicode code points); a section read out of a list
(`§§ 1981, 1983`) has no span of its own, so its offsets are null. A citation and its pinpoint are
one row however often the pair appears (`mentions` counts them), and different pinpoints of one
section are separate rows resolved and charged once. `counts.found` is rows,
`counts.distinctSections` is sections (the unit of price and cap). `includeUnresolved: false`
drops only rows that were sent to the resolver and did not resolve; `skipped` rows are always kept
and `counts` and the charge never change.

**Ranges.** A range (`§§ 2510-2523`, `§ 201 through 219`, `29 U.S.C. § 201-219`) returns its two
ends as rows marked `rangeRole` (`start` / `end`) with `rangePartner` naming the other end; each end
is resolved and charged as its own section. A short word range (plain section numbers, up to 25
between the ends) also lists the sections between as `rangeRole: interior`, `skipped:
range_interior` rows, which are never resolved or charged (`counts.interior`). A wider range, or a
hyphen range, returns its ends only and `notes` says so (browse between them with
`GET /us/statutes/divisions`). A list stops where the next citation starts, so
`42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1983 and 28 U.S.C. § 1331` is three citations.

**Pinpoints.** A citation printed with a pinpoint also carries `pinpointMatch`, the unit it names
located inside the resolved section, as on `GET /us/statutes/resolve`, at no extra cost and for at
most about 20 seconds per call. Read `pinpointMatch.matched` first: `false` (or `matchLevel`
`ancestor` or `none`) says the section has no such unit, and `structure.quality: heuristic` says the
outline was parsed from the text and failed a check. A unit that exists is not proof it says what
your text claims: compare `pinpointMatch.text` with the claim. A row whose pinpoint could not be
looked up keeps its resolution and gets a `pinpointNote`.

**Unresolved rows** carry `missReason`, `candidates` and `missReasonHint`, as on
`GET /us/statutes/resolve`, at no extra charge.

get.description:
Resolve a Bluebook citation to the section it names, confirmed against the corpus, with an
official source link. Pass it as `cite`: `42 U.S.C. 1983`, `16 C.F.R. 444.1` or
`Del. Code Ann. tit. 13, 1301`.

**Cost**: 2 credits per call, charged whether or not the citation resolves, because a confident
"this citation does not resolve" is the answer you want when verifying a citation an LLM produced.
Refunded on a failure and on a citation we could not read or that names no jurisdiction
(`missReason` `malformed` or `ambiguous_jurisdiction`; retry the ambiguous one with `state`),
where `creditsConsumed` is 0.

When the citation resolves, `resolved` is `true` and `section` carries the full metadata (the shape
of `/us/statutes/section/{actId}`). When it does not, `resolved` is `false` and `section` is `null`:
treat that as "unverified", not "current". `matchLevel` says when `section` is not the exact unit
you cited (`container`, `multiple`, `repaired`) and `missReason` says why a citation did not
resolve; both are described on their fields. A pinpoint (`625 ILCS 5/11-601(c)`, `42 U.S.C.
1983(b)(2)`) resolves to its parent section, is echoed in `subsection` and is located inside the
section in `pinpoint` at no extra credits. Read `pinpoint.matched` first: a pinpoint the section
does not contain is reported as `matched: false` with the units that do exist, never answered
with the whole section. A state code container cited with its container word (`8 Del. C. ch. 1,
subch. VII`) answers its first section with `matchLevel: container`.

A citation to a STATE session law (an act as enacted, for example `CHAPTER 2025-12` or `S.F.No. 1552`) names no code section, so `resolved` stays `false` and `section` stays `null`. The law is described in `sessionLaw`, beside `matchedCorpus: "session_law"`, with an `href` to read it under `/us/session-laws`, and enough to answer what it is and when it took effect without a second call: `title`, `billNumber`, `approvedDate`, `effectiveFirst` and `effectiveLast` (null when the publisher prints no effective date), `enactmentOutcome` and `sourceUrl`, the government publisher's own text. A citation naming several laws comes back `ambiguous` with every candidate and none chosen for you. A `state` scope applies to session laws; a `corpusType` scope excludes them. No extra charge, and a citation that resolves to a section is never checked against session laws. A citation that names no state is matched against every state's laws, so at most 25 of them are checked per call: the others carry no `sessionLaw` block, which says nothing about whether the law exists. Name the state, or send the rest in another call.


**Bounded rows.** A heavily amended section (26 U.S.C. 1) carries hundreds of references and a credit line of tens of thousands of characters. Each row keeps the first 50 items of every long list and the first 4,000 characters of `history` and `committeeNote`. A row that was cut carries `responseBounds` (`truncated`, and per field the `total`, what was `returned` and `nextOffset`); a row that was not cut omits it. The whole record is one call away: `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}?full=true`.

post.description:
Search US federal and state law and get back the most relevant sections, with citations and
links to the official source documents. State session laws (acts as enacted) are at
`/us/session-laws`.

Scope a search with `corpusType` (the field lists every token). `GET /us/statutes/coverage`
shows what is held per jurisdiction and corpus; the
[Coverage page](https://www.vaquill.ai/docs/api-guide/coverage) explains it. Narrow further with
`state`, `code`, `article`, `titleNumber`, `chapter` and `part`, and for `AGENCY_GUIDANCE` with
`source`. Pass `corpusType` whenever you know it: an unscoped query can surface keyword matches
from unrelated corpora.

**Cost**: 4 credits per call. Refunded on a failure, on a page served with
`rankingDegraded: true` (the relevance model was down), and on a filtered search that matches no
section (a `notes` entry names the filters). A search that ran in full and found nothing on point
(`noGoodMatch: true`) is charged, because the work was done; its rows are the nearest sections,
not matches, so check `noGoodMatch` and `matchQuality` before using them. A 422 is never charged.

`includeBody: true` returns each hit's full text inline on `body`, at the ordinary 6-credit body
price per row that returns text. If your balance cannot cover every body, the rows it can cover
are served and charged in rank order and the rest carry `bodyNote: insufficient_credits`. Read
`creditsConsumed`. `includePinpoint: true` names the subsection each hit matched, in `pinpoints`
keyed by `actId`, at no extra cost. Both switches are described on their fields.

`matchType` is `any` (default, hybrid semantic and keyword), `all`, `phrase` or `boolean` (a
terms-and-connectors expression; the operators are listed on that field). Pass a citation as the
`query` (e.g. `42 U.S.C. § 1983`) and it resolves to rank 1 at `relevanceScore: 1.0`; if you
already know the citation, `GET /us/statutes/resolve` returns the same section for less.

**Pagination**: `limit` is at most 50. With `matchType: "any"`, `offset` is at most 70 and ranked
results come from a bounded pool, so about 60 to 90 results are reachable and `hasMore` turns
false at the end of it. With `boolean`, `all` or `phrase`, `offset` goes up to 10,000;
follow `nextOffset` until `hasMore` is false. A later page can hold fewer rows than `limit`,
because candidates outside your filters or failing full-text verification are left out. Every
page of one query slices one ranking, so results never repeat or go missing across pages.
`count` is the size of the current page, not a corpus-wide total (`total` is a deprecated alias
for `count`).

get.description:
Get the full text of a statute section as plain text and, where the source has markup, HTML. Works
across USC, CFR and state corpora; the text keeps the formatting, cross-references and paragraph
numbering of the official source.

**Cost**: 6 credits per call. Refunded when no text is returned: a 404, a failure, a section whose
text is not yet ingested (`available: false`), a section the publisher prints as images
(`bodyUnavailable: true`) and an `asOf` date we hold no text for. A citation in the `actId` slot
adds the 2-credit `/resolve` price (8 in all, reported in `creditsConsumed`); the 2 are kept even
when the text turns out unavailable, because the citation was resolved. Send the `actId` itself
to avoid them.

**Response**: `available: true` with `html` and `plain`, or `available: false` with a `note` and
`creditsConsumed: 0` when the text is not yet ingested (metadata stays on
`/us/statutes/section/{actId}`). Where the source is markup (the U.S. Code, eCFR, the state portals
we mirror) `html` is the publisher's sanitised markup. A section held only as text has the same
text in `html` wrapped in paragraph markup, so `format=both` carries it twice: send `format=plain`
to receive it once. `sourceUrl` is where the government published the text: cite and verify
against it, not against `source`, which names our storage backend. It is null when we hold no
official link for the section.

**A section with no text to return.** Appendices, forms and maps that the publisher prints as
images answer `available: false`, `plain` and `html` null, `bodyUnavailable: true`,
`bodyUnavailableReason: "image_only_source"`, a `note` and `creditsConsumed: 0`. That is a final
answer, not a failure to retry: the section exists and its metadata is complete. Search rows,
`includeBody` and `POST /sections` carry the same two fields, with `body` null and no body charge
for that row.

**Tables and figures.** Where a section has a structured rendering, `source` is `r2_render` and
tables and figures keep their position: `html` has `<table>` and `<figure>` elements, `markdown`
(only for `format=all` or `markdown`) has pipe tables and `![alt](url)`, and `plain` has
tab-separated rows and `[Figure N: caption]`. `tables` and `figures` list them in document order,
with `hasTables` and `hasFigures` flags. `tables: null` means not known (the corpus has no
structured rendering), not none. The price is the same for every `format`.

**Law versus apparatus (`content`, `sourceCredit`, `notes`).** `plain` and `html` are the whole
body as the publisher prints it: the operative text, the source credit, then the notes apparatus
(historical and revision notes, committee reports, amendments). For United States Code sections
most of that body is apparatus, so the section is also split into `content` (the operative text
only), `sourceCredit` and `notes`. Send `content` to a model: the full body invites it to quote
an old amendment note as the law in force. `format=content` returns the three split fields instead
of `plain` and `html`; `format=operative` drops `notes` as well. The price does not change; it
saves bandwidth and prompt budget. USC only: on CFR and state corpora the split fields are null
(never "empty section") and both formats fall back to `plain` with a `note`.

**Subsections.** `structured=true` adds a `subsections` tree addressable by pincite, and
`markdown` as nested lists. `pinpoint=(c)(1)` returns that one unit in `pinpoint` alongside the
body: labels outermost first, without the section number, and a label with a hyphen or dot is a
single label (`(f)(1.5)`). Read `pinpoint.matched` first. The two combine, at no extra cost, and
neither can be combined with `asOf`. A malformed pinpoint is a 422 and is not charged. `structure`
says whether the outline is a stored artifact checked against this exact text or was parsed on
this request.

**Point-in-time (`asOf=YYYY-MM-DD`).** Same cost. Returns the text as it stood on that date, as
`plain` only (never `html`). `asOf.engine` says which of two engines answered, and they make
different promises.

- `stored_edition` (CFR annual editions, the US Code, the Copyright Compendium, OFAC FAQs): a
  printed edition returned verbatim, and `isBounded: true` means your date fell inside an edition
  we hold. Coverage is enumerated, not continuous: a date in a gap between held editions returns
  `source: "unavailable"`, no text and an `outOfCoverageReason` naming what we do hold, and is
  refunded. For the US Code most historical dates fall in a gap today.
- `observed_change` (every other corpus): a reconstruction, not an archive. The corpus holds one
  current text per citation, and an earlier one is rebuilt from the before-side of the first change
  we observed after your date. `source` is `live`, `reconstructed` or `unavailable` (refunded).
  Here `isBounded: true` is the weak claim that we observed no change affecting your date, not
  that there was none, because capture began long after the corpus did.

If your date precedes the current text's effective date, today's text is never returned as the law
on that date: you get a held prior version or `source: "unavailable"` with
`currentVersionEffective` and `earliestHeldVersion` and no text. A section that states no readable
effective date and has no capture reaching your date returns today's text with a `note` saying it
is unverified for that date. `basisChangeId` names the change event the answer rests on (readable at
`/us/statutes/section/{actId}/changes`) and `observedFrom` how far back the evidence reaches. A
section that did not exist on that date returns `available: false` with `asOf.existed: false` and
is charged, because a confident negative is the answer. A date later than today (UTC) is a 422 and
is not charged.

parameters.description:
Which representations to return. `both` (the default) returns `html` and `plain`. A long section carries the same text twice that way, so `plain` or `html` alone roughly halves the payload. Cost is unchanged: the fetch is the same either way.

`all` adds `markdown` where the section has a structured rendering. It is opt-in because it is a third full copy of the text (about 600,000 extra characters on `49 CFR 172.101`), which a model-facing client would pay for in tokens without asking.

`markdown` returns only `markdown`. On a section with no structured rendering it falls back to `plain` with a `note` saying so, never to an empty body. `tables` and `figures` are returned on every format, because they are small and describe the text you received.

`content` omits `html` and `plain` and returns the split fields (`content`, `sourceCredit`, `notes`).

`operative` omits `notes` as well, leaving `content` + `sourceCredit`: the law and what enacted it, and nothing else. This is the smallest representation of a section, and on a note-heavy section it is the difference between a payload that fits in a prompt and one that does not. Measured on `17 U.S.C. § 107`: 95,217 bytes at `both`, 30,545 at `content`, 1,564 at `operative`, all for the same 6 credits.

Only United States Code sections can be split, so on any other corpus both values fall back to returning `plain` with a `note` saying why -- `content` will be null there, so read `note` rather than assuming the section was empty.

get.description:
Every change our refreshes have observed to one section: when it was added,
each time its text was replaced, and whether it has since been removed.

**Cost**: 1 credit. Not-found and failed lookups are not charged. An empty
history for a section that exists IS the answer and is charged.

A section lookup tells you what the law says today. This tells you whether that
is the same thing it said when you last reviewed it. Unlike a board watch, which
can only show changes that postdate the subscription, this reads the history
already captured.

**What this is, and is not.** These are OBSERVED changes: a refresh compared
the source against the copy we held and found it different. `detectedAt` is
when we saw it, an upper bound on when it took effect, never the effective date
itself. For the publisher's own effective and amendment dates, read
`amendmentHistory` on `GET /us/statutes/section/{act_id}`. The two are
complements: the publisher tells you what it says changed, this tells you what
actually moved and when we could have told you.

**Coverage is bounded by capture, not by the age of the law.** Change capture
began long after the corpus itself did, it is per-source, and events are swept
at 5 years. An empty `changes` list therefore means *no captured change*, not
*never amended*. The `coverage` field on every response says so; surface it
rather than rendering an empty list as "unchanged".

**This is not legislative history.** It lists only changes Vaquill's own refreshes recorded. For the
acts that amended a section over the years read `GET /us/statutes/section/{act_id}/enactments`
(state session laws, where supported) and `amendmentHistory` on the section record. When the log is
empty, `note` says so and points there.

**A removed section still answers.** When the newest change is a `removed`, the
section is gone from the corpus and `section` comes back null. That is a
successful, charged response, not a 404 -- learning that a provision was
repealed is the point.

**Paging.** `hasMore` is true only when at least one more change sits behind this page (the route reads one row past `limit` to know). `total` is the size of this page, not a corpus-wide count. Walk backwards
through history with `beforeId` (the smallest `id` you hold) and forward into

get.description:
The USC and CFR sections whose text cross-references a given section.

**Cost**: 2 credits. Not-found, failed lookups, and sections in a corpus with no
cross-reference index are not charged.

A section lookup tells you what a section cites; this is the other direction,
which provisions elsewhere in the code depend on this one. That is the question
behind "if this section changes, what else is affected".

Results are one row per citing section, never one row per matching chunk, best
first. A section whose own text was read and does not name this one is dropped,
not listed. Order: sections whose own text is confirmed to name this one, then by closeness
to it (same chapter, same title, same code, other federal law, everything
else), then by how focused the citing section is. A tax-code list that mentions
a statute in passing ranks below the chapter that implements it.

**Paging**: `limit` is the page size (default 25, max 100) and `offset` the
start. Read `hasMore` and pass `nextOffset` back as `offset` for the next page;
`total` and `totalCiters` are the number of citing sections found (the
size of this page is `returned`). It is the whole count only
when `totalCitersIsLowerBound` is false. At most 5,000 candidates are read per
call (the most-cited sections measured have about 3,000);
when `totalCitersIsLowerBound` is true there are more citers than that, and the
ranking covers only the slice that was read (in storage order), so a citer
outside it can be missing from every page. Every page is priced as one call.

**Scope**: USC and CFR. State codes and Federal Register rules carry no
section-level cross-reference index, so a section from either returns an empty
list with a `note` explaining why, and is refunded. When `note` is null, an
empty `citers` is a real answer: plenty of sections are cited by nothing.

**Completeness**: this reads references as the publisher wrote them, including
the title-relative form a section uses for its own neighbours. A citation that
the source never recorded in machine-readable form cannot appear here, so treat
a result as evidence of a citation rather than proof there are no others.

get.description:
Provisions in other states that address the same subject as a given state
statute section.

**Cost**: 6 credits. Not-found, failed lookups, sections outside the state
statute corpus, calls where no other state holds a comparable provision
(empty `neighbors`, with a `note`), and calls whose relevance ranking was
unavailable (`rankingDegraded: true`) are not charged.

Every state words and numbers its provisions differently, so comparing a rule
across jurisdictions normally means running one search per state and reconciling
the results by hand. This starts from one section you already have and returns
the comparable provision elsewhere.

**At most one provision per state**, most similar first, so the response reads
as a jurisdiction comparison rather than a relevance list. Every other
jurisdiction is searched; `statesCovered` is how many of them were actually
examined (held something to consider), not how many appear in `neighbors`. A state whose best provision is
not on the same subject is left out rather than padded in (nothing scoring below
0.55 is served), and definitions, short-title and statement-of-purpose sections
are never offered as the comparable provision of a substantive section.
Historical editions and repealed or superseded provisions are never offered.

**Scope**: state statute sections only. USC, CFR, state regulations, court
rules, constitutions and every other corpus return empty with a `note`,
refunded, since only a state statute has a state-statute analogue.

**`rankingDegraded`**: when the relevance model is unavailable the neighbours
come back in retrieval order, `similarity` is a retrieval score on a much
smaller scale than 0-1 and `matchQuality` is null. The call is then free
(`creditsConsumed` 0): retry shortly for the ranked answer.

**What `similarity` is**: a retrieval score between 0 and 1, describing how
closely two provisions read. It is not a legal opinion. A high score means the
provisions cover the same ground, never that they impose the same obligation,
and the differences are usually the point. Treat this as the shortlist to read,
not the answer. Each neighbour also carries `matchQuality` (`strong`,
`moderate` or `weak`), the same tier names `POST /us/statutes/search` uses, read
off the relevance score: lead with `strong` and `moderate`. A state with nothing
comparable is left out, and a section with no comparable provision anywhere
answers with an empty `neighbors` and a `note`.

get.description:
The term definitions that apply to a section: the ones the section defines in
its own text, and the ones parsed from its chapter's definitions section.

**Cost**: 4 credits. Not-found, failed lookups, and calls that return no terms
(no definitions in the section's own text and none in the chapter, or a
definitions section whose text is not yet ingested) are all refunded.

A statute's terms of art are defined in a separate section elsewhere in the
chapter, not in the provision you are reading: "person" routinely includes
corporations, "employee" routinely excludes independent contractors. This
resolves that section and returns its terms.

Many provisions define a term for themselves instead: `As used in this
section, "security" means ...`. Those come back first with `source: section`
and a `pinpoint` naming the subdivision that carries the definition (`(b)`), so
it can be cited to that subdivision. Only a quoted term with a scope phrase
("as used in this section") or opening a sentence or labelled unit counts;
ordinary prose that happens to use "means" is not read as a definition. The
section's own text is checked in every supported corpus, including ones with no
chapter to scope a definitions section to.

Terms from the chapter's definitions section carry `source:
definitions_section`; `definitionsSection` names where those came from, so a
definition can be quoted and cited to the provision that actually carries it.

**Scope**: strongest on the U.S. Code, where a chapter's definitions section is
conventionally structured and parses reliably. CFR and state codes are
best-effort: publishers format definitions inconsistently, and a definitions
section we can locate but not parse into terms returns empty with a `note` and
is refunded. `definitionsSection` is still populated in that case, so you can
fetch its text directly from `/section/{actId}/body` and read it yourself.

You are never charged for a chapter whose terms we could not return.

get.description:
The state session laws a publisher's own tables list against one code section: which act added,
amended or repealed it, when the act took effect, and what the publisher printed. Start from an
`actId` (or a citation), then read the act at `href`, or its text at `href` plus `/body`.

**Stage 1.** This reads the code-section tables that state publishers print against their session
laws ("sections affected") through a reverse lookup. It is never a complete amendment history: only
acts we hold, in sessions we hold (`coverage.sessionsHeld`), whose table lists the section in the
printed form we map. An empty `enactments` with `supported: true` means "no held table lists this
section", not "this section was never amended". `coverage.note` says per jurisdiction what is not
read. Rows are newest act first and one per act; the section record's own `history` field names
only the latest amendment, so a section can show one act there and many here.

**Two kinds of evidence, never blended.** `basis: publisher_sections_affected` with
`matchQuality: as_printed` comes from the publisher's table. In AR, LA, ME, MI, VT, WI there is no such table
read, so the section's history credit line is read instead: `basis: credit_line` with
`matchQuality: credit_cite_unique` means the credit cites a session law (`citeAsPrinted`, verbatim)
that names exactly one act we hold, in the same state, in a year that fits. A citation that fits
several acts, a special-session or list form, or an act we do not hold is dropped, not guessed. A
credit-line row states no action (`action: other`).

**Where it works.** CA, DC, HI, KY, MO, MS, NE, UT, WA: the jurisdictions where the publisher's printed form was shown to
map to our section numbers against real data on both sides. Any other jurisdiction (and any
federal, regulation or constitution section) answers `supported: false`, an empty list, a `reason`
and a `coverage.note`, and is not charged. Matching is on the whole number after folding case,
spacing, dashes and the section sign (`71-24,104` does not match `71-24,10`); where a publisher
qualifies a section by code (California, Hawaii, DC) the code must match too.

**Cost**: 1 credit per call. Refunded on a 404, on an unsupported jurisdiction or section,
and on a failure (500, 503). A supported section whose answer is empty is charged, because "no held
table lists it" is the answer you paid for. A citation in place of the id also pays the `/resolve`
price when it resolves; a citation that resolves to nothing is refunded in full, that price
included. `creditsConsumed` reports what was billed.

**A row.** `sessionLawId` and `href` name the act. `action` is `added | amended | repealed |
renumbered | other`, mapped only where the publisher's legend is settled, and `actionAsPrinted` is
always the publisher's own code. `effectiveDates` are the act's, not necessarily this section's.
`sectionAsPrinted`, `codeAsPrinted` and `actSectionAsPrinted` are verbatim. An act whose table lists
the section more than once with the same action is folded into one row, and `printedEntryCount`
says how many entries it holds. An omnibus act is titled by every section it amends (California):
such a `title` is shortened to the section you asked about, `titleCompacted` is true and
`sectionsTouchedCount` says how many sections the title lists; the full title is at `href`.
`truncated` is true past 200 rows.

**Example**

```bash
curl "https://api.vaquill.ai/api/v1/us/statutes/section/STATE_MS_T27_C71_S27-71-5/enactments" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VAQUILL_API_KEY"
```

**Related endpoints**

- `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}/changes` is what our refreshes observed to the section.
- `GET /us/session-laws/{sessionLawId}` reads an act from `href`; `/body` reads its text.
- `GET /us/statutes/coverage` says which sessions we hold in each jurisdiction's `sessionLaws`
  block.

get.description:
The sections immediately before and after a given section, in statutory order.

**Cost**: 2 credits. Not-found and failed lookups are not charged, and neither is an
answer with no neighbour on either side (`note` says why it is empty).

Search cannot answer "what comes next", because relevance ranking is not
statutory order: the definitions a section relies on usually sit a few sections
back and its exceptions a few forward.

Neighbours never cross the containing chapter (or, where a section has no
chapter, the containing title or state code), so you get the sections a reader
would actually turn to, not the numerically adjacent row from an unrelated part
of the corpus.

Neighbours stay within ONE container: the first section of a chapter has an empty
`previous` and the last has an empty `next`, even when the code continues in the
adjacent chapter, part or title (which are not traversed). When that is why a
side is empty, `note` says so, so an empty side is not read as the start or end
of the whole code. Superseded or not-yet-effective versions of a section are
never returned as neighbours, and a section is never its own neighbour.

Ordering is natural, not lexicographic: `9` before `10`, `240.9` before
`240.10`, `1983` before `1983a`.

get.description:
Federal Register documents linked to one CFR section, from two signals.

**Cost**: 2 credits. Not-found and failed lookups are not charged. An `act_id` sent as a
citation (`21 CFR 314.50`) instead of a CFR act id adds the 2-credit `/resolve` fee, kept when the
citation does not resolve.

`printed_note`: the section's printed source note cites `83 FR 1234`, and a Federal Register rule
of the same CFR title and part spans that page of that volume and was published on the date printed.
Pre-1994 citations (`legacyPrintedCitations`) are kept as text and never resolved. `date_join`: a rule referencing the section's
CFR title and part took effect (or was published) on a date eCFR records as an amendment of this
section. `matchBasis` says which; `quality` is `verified` only when both agree and `candidate`
otherwise. Each eCFR version row in `versions` gets a tier: `confirmed`, `candidate` (one date match), `ambiguous` (two or more documents, none picked), `unmatched` (searched, found nothing) or `not_searched` (older than the date-join window, never looked at). A document found only in the printed note, with no version row meeting its dates, is `candidate` in both `quality` and `tier`. Corrections are attached to their parent in `corrections`. A candidate is a lead, not a finding: a rule that touches the part on the same day as
an amendment may not be the one that amended this section. `matchReason` says so on a candidate
that matched on title, part and date only and does not name the section.

**A printed note can be stale.** `noteIsStale` is true when eCFR records an amendment later than
the newest dated citation the note prints. Newer documents then appear only as `date_join`
candidates. `unresolvedCitations` lists printed citations we could not match to a document;
that is absence in our corpus, never proof the citation is wrong. Read `coverage`.

Metadata for up to 50 sections in one call.

**Cost**: 2 credits **per section returned**. Identifiers with no match

not a citation (an unknown id such as `NOPE1`, punctuation, an over-long
string) is a plain miss and costs nothing; a real citation sent in place
of an id pays the `/resolve` price on top when it resolves, and nothing when
it does not.

`sections` preserves the order of `actIds` for the sections it returns, and
misses are reported separately in `notFound`, one entry per miss (a miss is
never listed twice and never appears in `sections`). Because misses are
dropped from `sections`, and two inputs naming one section (a citation beside
its id) are served once, `sections` is NOT index-aligned with `actIds`: match
each section to its input by `actId`, or through `resolved` (its `input` and
`actId`) for a citation. An id whose code is still being read comes back in

most 200 characters; a blank id and an unknown request key are refused with a

post.description:
Subscribe to a board. `webhookUrl` is validated against an SSRF blocklist (loopback, private, link-local and cloud-metadata ranges) before acceptance and again on every dispatch. Every `board.updated` delivery body carries a `deliveryId`, stable per watch per refresh event even across our own retries, so you can dedupe on it.

Each item in the body's `changes[]` carries the same `id` and `detectedAt` as `GET /watches/{watchId}/changes`. Pass its `id` as `sinceId` to page the rest of a change set that overflowed `changesOverflowCount`, or to `GET /watches/{watchId}/changes/{changeId}/diff` for the before and after text.

The body carries two sets of counters over different populations. Read `sections*`, and read `rows*` only if you already built on it:

- `sectionsAdded` / `sectionsAmended` / `sectionsRemoved` count sections, one per change event, the same unit as `changes[]`. They are narrowed by this watch's `scope`, which the body echoes back, and omitted when the refresh classified no change events.
- `rowsAdded` / `rowsUpdated` / `rowsDeleted` are the refresh's raw storage counters for the whole board. They are never narrowed by `scope` and do not share a unit with each other: added and deleted count storage chunks, updated counts sections. A watch scoped to 21 CFR part 314 can receive `rowsUpdated: 480` next to `sectionsAmended: 1`. Do not present the `rows*` keys as three populations of sections.

Free.

An empty list means no captured change, not that the law was never amended; the publisher's own history, where there is one, is on the section's `amendmentHistory`. The endpoint is read-only and safe to poll alongside a webhook or email watch: it cannot suppress, advance or double-fire a delivery.

Paging: pass `sinceId` with `meta.cursor` from your previous page to get only what is new, and keep going while `meta.hasMore` is true. `changeKind` is `added` (a new section), `amended` (its content was replaced), or `removed` (it disappeared from a full refresh of the source). `citation` and `title` are null for corpora that do not carry them. `detectedAt` is when our refresh saw the change; `sourceChangedOn`, the publisher's own date, is carried on `cfr`, `federal_rules` and on no other board, and its absence never licenses reading `detectedAt` as the amendment date. Check `publishesSourceChangedOn` on `GET /boards`.

get.description:
The section's text before and after this specific change, when available (see `hasDiff` on the change list above).

How many sides a change has depends on its kind, and each is a complete answer:

- `amended`: both sides. This is the only kind where one side alone is not a partial answer but no answer.
- `added`: after side only. There is no before side by definition, and the full text of a newly published section is precisely what the notification is for.
- `removed`: before side only, the last text we held.

A missing side is not an error: `hasBefore`/`hasAfter` say which text is actually present, and `diffAvailable` (with `unavailableReason` when false) says whether there is a diff at all, so a caller can render a graceful 'diff unavailable' state for older changes or a snapshot that failed to capture, instead of treating null as a failure.

Cost: 4 credits per call (see `/api-credits/pricing`). This is the only metered route in the alerts family: every other board and watch endpoint, including the `/changes` list this reads from, is free.

You are charged only for a diff that answers the question its kind asks, and `creditsConsumed` always reports what was actually billed. Refunded in full (`creditsConsumed: 0`): an `amended` change missing either side, an `amended` change whose two sides resolve to identical text (a capture artifact on our side, not a change on the publisher's), and any change resolving no text at all. A one-sided `added` or `removed` diff is the complete answer and is charged normally.

Test deliveries (`POST /watches/{id}/test`) never appear, as they are not persisted.

`consecutiveFailures` counts how many of the most recent attempts failed in a row, and `deliveryHealth` is `failing` once that reaches 3. Read them before reading the list: a watch can keep firing on schedule and delivering nothing, and the streak is the only field that distinguishes that from a bad day. `consecutiveFailuresTruncated` is true when the streak fills the whole page, meaning the real run is at least this long. `deliveryHealth` is `blocked` when the newest attempt was not sent because the account's plan no longer includes webhook delivery (Business); the row's `error` says so. Page back with `beforeId` = `meta.nextBeforeId`.

Nothing notifies you when a webhook starts failing, so poll this route. We alert ourselves after 3 consecutive failures, but we send you no email and no callback, and a failing receiver is in your infrastructure rather than ours. A watch stays active and keeps being dispatched while every delivery fails, so silence from your endpoint is not evidence that the law did not change. Check `deliveryHealth` on a schedule of your own.

`error` on each attempt says why it failed, including the redirect target when an endpoint answered 3xx. Deliveries do not follow redirects: a 3xx is a failed delivery, not a delivered one, so register the endpoint's final URL.

Free.

tags.description:
Search and retrieve US primary law. Covers the United States Code and the Statutes at Large, the Code of Federal Regulations and its annual editions, state statutory codes and administrative regulations, federal and state constitutions, court rules, Federal Register rules and Presidential documents, federal and state agency guidance, agency adjudications, state Attorney General opinions, the Sentencing Guidelines and US tax treaties. Scope a search with the `corpusType` filter, and call `/us/statutes/coverage` for the live jurisdiction-by-corpusType list.

- **Search**: Search across all USC, CFR, state, and regulatory sections
- **Section**: Get metadata, citation, hierarchy, and source links for a specific section
- **Body**: Get the full text of a section
- **Enactments**: Which state session laws a publisher's own tables list against a section (supported jurisdictions only, never a complete history)
tags.name: US Statutes

tags.description:
State session laws: the acts of each legislature as they were enacted, chapter by chapter, before they are folded into a code. A session law is what the governor signs. It carries the act's own text, including the language it strikes and inserts, its approval and effective dates, and, where the publisher prints one, the code sections it changes. That makes it the source for "which act changed this section, and when did it take effect".

Every act has a permanent `sessionLawId` (for example `SSL_MN_2025R_G_Y2025_C1`, Minnesota Laws 2025, regular session, chapter 1) whether or not we hold its text, and a citation or bill number such as `S.F.No. 1552` is accepted where an id goes. v1 serves STATE acts only. Federal session laws (the Statutes at Large, `SAL_` ids) are served by `/us/statutes/section`, and `/us/statutes/resolve` points a session-law citation here.

**Start here**: check `/us/statutes/coverage` (free) for what we hold per state: each jurisdiction's `sessionLaws` block lists its sessions, which are complete or only partly collected, and the `series` and `instrumentTypes` that exist. Then **List** a session or a date range to get ids, **Get** one act for its record, then **Body** for its text. A law missing from a partly collected session is a free 404 (`session_not_fully_collected`), not proof it does not exist.

- **List**: everything enacted in a state's session, approved in a window, or taking effect on a date
- **Get**: one act by id or by citation; dates (`effectiveDates` is always a list), sources and the code sections it affects
- **Body**: the act's text as printed, paged by cursor, with amendatory markup preserved where the publisher printed it
- **Batch**: up to 50 ids or citations in one call, the same record as Get, billed per law served, with every miss listed and its reason
- **Changes**: a sync feed of the registry over an integer cursor (`sinceId`): what began to be served, was corrected, withdrawn or merged

The reverse link, from a code section to the acts a publisher's own tables list against it, is `GET /us/statutes/section/{actId}/enactments`.
tags.name: US Session Laws

tags.description:
How a federal rule is made, as public records tied together by its Regulation Identifier Number (RIN): the semiannual Unified Agenda (every edition from Fall 1995), the OIRA review under Executive Order 12866, the Regulations.gov docket and its documents, and the Federal Register documents that proposed and finalised it.

**Start here**: `GET /us/rulemaking/coverage` (free) lists what is held per source and whether each is fresh. Then **By RIN** for everything held for one rule, **Agenda history** for how its timetable moved edition by edition, or **Dockets** and **Documents** for the Regulations.gov side.

Every link between sources carries its `basis` and `quality` (`verified`, `candidate`, `ambiguous`). A link we could not make with confidence is marked, never guessed, and an umbrella RIN shared by unrelated rules claims no proposal-to-final pairing. A comment count of `null` means not measured, never zero. Comment text, attachments and commenter information are not held or served.
tags.name: US Rulemaking

tags.description:
Law-change alerts. Subscribe to a **board** (a tracked corpus source, identified by `corpusType` plus an optional `state`) and get a webhook or email whenever it refreshes with real changes, naming the exact sections that changed. Fetch old-vs-new text for any amended section via the change diff.

Boards refresh on their own existing cadence; watching one does not change how often it refreshes. Every endpoint here is **free**: authenticated by API key and rate-limited, but not credit-metered.

See the [Law Change Alerts guide](https://www.vaquill.ai/docs/api-guide/alerts) for the full walkthrough.

post.description:
Sent by `POST /watches/{watchId}/test`, signed and authenticated exactly like a real delivery. Headers: `Content-Type: application/json`, `X-Vaquill-Event: board.test`.

**Verification.** Present only when the watch has a `webhookSecret`. Prefer the Standard Webhooks headers: `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` (Unix seconds) and `webhook-signature` (`v1,<base64>`, several space separated while a secret rotates), an HMAC-SHA256 over `{webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{raw body}`. The HMAC key is the base64 decoding of the secret after `whsec_` when it has that prefix, otherwise the secret's UTF-8 bytes. Verify against the raw bytes before parsing, and reject a timestamp more than 5 minutes old. `webhook-id` is stable across retries of one delivery. The legacy `X-Vaquill-Signature: sha256=<hex>` header (HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body) is also sent, is deprecated, and remains for at least 12 months. Respond with any 2xx to acknowledge; redirects are not followed.
